title: Spectral Properties And Coding Transitions Of Haar-Random Quantum Codes
authors: Grace M. Sommers, J. Alexander Jacoby, Zack Weinstein, David A. Huse, And Sarang Gopalakrishnan
abstract:
Author(s): Grace M. Sommers, J. Alexander Jacoby, Zack Weinstein, David A. Huse, and Sarang Gopalakrishnan

An investigation of Haar-random quantum codes reveals a simple mechanism for the transition between decodable and nondecodable phases of quantum codes under local noise.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020328] Published Wed May 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper investigates Haar-random quantum codes and identifies a simple mechanism for the transition between decodable and non-decodable phases under local noise.
motivation: Understanding the robustness of quantum error-correcting codes against local noise is crucial for practical quantum computing. The paper aims to characterize the spectral properties and coding transitions of random quantum codes.
method: The authors analyze Haar-random quantum codes using statistical physics methods, mapping the decoding problem to a statistical mechanics model and studying its phase transitions.
result: They find a sharp transition between decodable and non-decodable phases as a function of noise strength, and characterize the spectral properties of the code's density matrix.
conclusion: The work provides insight into the fundamental limits of quantum error correction and suggests that random codes can achieve optimal thresholds under certain conditions.

title: Quantum Cryptography Beyond Key Distribution: Theory And Experiment
authors: Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, And Philip Walther
abstract:
Author(s): Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, and Philip Walther

Cryptography not only involves the sending of secret messages but also encompasses many protocols and procedures that provide privacy and security in the networked world. Likewise, quantum resources have the potential to enhance cryptography in ways that go beyond the well-known example of quantum key distribution. This review offers a classification of the main crypto primitives that are available quantum mechanically. It explains the security that they offer, including the sometimes significant limitations on their theoretical capabilities. Implementations using current photonic techniques are discussed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045006] Published Fri Dec 19, 2025.
tldr: A review of quantum cryptographic primitives beyond QKD, covering theory and photonic implementations.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive classification and security analysis of quantum cryptography protocols beyond key distribution, addressing the need for a structured overview.
method: The paper reviews and categorizes quantum cryptographic primitives, explains their security guarantees and limitations, and discusses experimental implementations using photonic platforms.
result: It presents a taxonomy of quantum cryptographic protocols and highlights the current experimental capabilities and challenges.
conclusion: Quantum cryptography offers a rich set of primitives beyond QKD, but practical implementations face significant limitations that require further research.

title: Active Quantum Reservoir Engineering: Using A Qubit To Manipulate Its Environment
authors: Marcelo Janovitch, Matteo Brunelli, And Patrick P. Potts
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2143 (2026).

Quantum reservoir engineering leverages dissipative processes to achieve desired behaviour, with applications ranging from entanglement generation to quantum error correction. Therein, a structured environment acts as an entropy sink for the system and no time-dependent control over the system is required. We develop a theoretical framework for active reservoir engineering, where time-dependent control over a quantum system is used to manipulate its environment. In this case, the system may act as an entropy sink for the environment. Our framework captures the dynamical interplay between system and environment, and provides an intuitive picture of how finite-size effects and system-environment correlations allow for manipulating the environment by repeated initialisation of the quantum system. We illustrate our results with two examples: a superconducting qubit coupled to an environment of two-level systems and a semiconducting quantum dot coupled to nuclear spins. In both scenarios, we find qualitative agreement with previous experimental results, illustrating how active control can unlock new functionalities in open quantum systems.

.
tldr: A theoretical framework for active reservoir engineering where time-dependent control over a quantum system manipulates its environment, illustrated with superconducting and semiconducting examples.
motivation: Standard quantum reservoir engineering uses structured environments as entropy sinks, but active control can unlock new functionalities by allowing the system to act as an entropy sink for the environment.
method: Develops a framework capturing dynamical interplay between system and environment, including finite-size effects and correlations, and applies it to two example systems: a superconducting qubit coupled to two-level systems and a quantum dot coupled to nuclear spins.
result: Qualitative agreement with previous experimental results is found, demonstrating that repeated initialization of the quantum system can manipulate the environment.
conclusion: Active control in open quantum systems enables new functionalities for reservoir engineering, with potential applications in quantum thermodynamics and information processing.

title: Decoupling Local Classicality From Classical Explainability: A Noncontextual Model For Bilocal Classical Theory And A Locally-classical But Contextual Theory
authors: Sina Soltani, Marco Erba, David Schmid, And John H.selby
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2142 (2026).

We construct an ontological model for the theory known as bilocal classical theory [1]. To our knowledge, this is only the second time that an ontological model has been constructed for an entire theory, rather than just for some particular scenarios within a theory. This result refutes a conjecture from [1] which suggested that there might be no local-realist ontological model for bilocal classical theory. Moreover, it is the first time that an ontological model has been constructed for a theory that fails to be locally tomographic, showing that the assumption of local tomography underpinning the structure theorem in [2] is a genuine limitation of the theorem. This demonstrates that in general there is no tension between failures of local tomography and classical explainability (i.e., generalised noncontextuality). In fact, bilocal classical theory is in many ways more simply understood via the underlying ontological model than it is within its original formulation (much as how odd-dimensional stabiliser subtheories can be more simply understood via Spekkens' toy theory). Furthermore, this result naturally leads to the question, does every locally-classical theory admit of an ontological model? By constructing a concrete counterexample, we show that this is not the case. Our findings demonstrate that there is no straightforward relationship between theories being locally-classical, and them being classically-explainable. This shows that the fundamental status of compositional properties (such as local tomography) is not a technical side-issue, but a central and unavoidable question for a coherent understanding even of classicality itself.

.
tldr: Constructs an ontological model for bilocal classical theory, refuting a conjecture and showing that local classicality does not imply classical explainability.
motivation: To understand the relationship between local classicality and classical explainability (generalized noncontextuality), and to test the necessity of local tomography for ontological models.
method: Constructs an explicit ontological model for bilocal classical theory using a hidden variable framework, and then builds a counterexample theory that is locally classical but contextual.
result: Bilocal classical theory admits a local-realist ontological model, contrary to a previous conjecture; moreover, there exist locally-classical theories that are contextual, decoupling the two properties.
conclusion: Compositional properties like local tomography are central to understanding classicality, and the relationship between local classicality and noncontextuality is not straightforward.

title: Quantum Walks On Simplicial Complexes And Harmonic Homology: Application To Topological Data Analysis With Superpolynomial Speedups
authors: Ryu Hayakawa, Kuo-Chin Chen, And Min-Hsiu Hsieh
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2138 (2026).

This work investigates whether quantum walks on simplicial complexes exhibit quantum advantages. We introduce a novel quantum walk that encodes the combinatorial Laplacian, a key object reflecting the topology of the simplicial complex. We construct a unitary encoding projecting onto the kernel of the Laplacian, representing the harmonic cycles in the complex's homology. Our efficient construction of quantum walk unitaries for clique complexes paves the way for exploring higher-order interactions within topological structures. Our construction requires [MATH] gates, where [MATH] is the number of vertices, [MATH] is the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian, and [MATH] is the projection error. Our results indicate apparent superpolynomial quantum speedup with quantum walks, without quantum oracles, provided the spectral gap of the Laplacian is inverse-polynomially bounded and efficient simplex sampling is available. Crucially, the walk operates on a state space encompassing both positively and negatively oriented simplices, effectively doubling its size compared to unoriented approaches. Through coherent interference of these paired simplices, we are able to successfully encode the combinatorial Laplacian, which would otherwise be impossible. This is our major technical contribution. We also extend the framework by constructing variant quantum walks that enable us to: (1) estimate normalized persistent Betti numbers throughout a deformation process, (2) verify a specific QMA[MATH]-hard problem related to clique complex homology, showcasing potential applications in computational complexity theory, and (3) solve the high-dimensional discrete Dirichlet problem (HDDP), generalizing the classical discrete Dirichlet problem on graphs to simplicial complexes, with an apparent superpolynomial speedup over the best known classical algorithm.

.
tldr: This paper introduces quantum walks on simplicial complexes that encode the combinatorial Laplacian, enabling superpolynomial speedups for topological data analysis and related problems.
motivation: Quantum walks on graphs have shown advantages, but extending them to simplicial complexes could unlock new quantum algorithms for topological data analysis and homology computation.
method: The authors construct a quantum walk that encodes the combinatorial Laplacian by operating on oriented simplices, using coherent interference to project onto harmonic cycles. They also build variants for persistent Betti numbers, QMA-hard problems, and the high-dimensional Dirichlet problem.
result: The construction achieves apparent superpolynomial quantum speedup without quantum oracles, assuming an inverse-polynomially bounded spectral gap and efficient simplex sampling.
conclusion: This work demonstrates that quantum walks on simplicial complexes can provide significant quantum advantages for topological data analysis and related computational problems.

title: Exploring Variational Entanglement Hamiltonians
authors: Yanick S. Kind And Benedikt Fauseweh
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2133 (2026).

Recent advances in analog and digital quantum-simulation platforms have enabled exploration of the spectrum of entanglement Hamiltonians via variational algorithms. In this work we analyze the convergence properties of the variationally obtained solutions and compare them to numerically exact calculations in quantum critical systems. We demonstrate that interpreting the cost functional as an integral permits the deployment of iterative quadrature schemes, thereby reducing the required number of measurements by more than an order of magnitude even in the presence of noise. We further show that a modified ansatz captures deviations from the Bisognano-Wichmann form in lattice models, improves convergence, improves trainability and provides a cost-function-level diagnostic for quantum phase transitions. Finally, we establish that a low cost value does not by itself guarantee convergence in trace distance. Nevertheless, it faithfully reproduces degeneracies and spectral gaps, which are essential for applications to topological phases.

.
tldr: This paper analyzes variational algorithms for learning entanglement Hamiltonians in quantum critical systems, demonstrating improved convergence and reduced measurements.
motivation: Understanding entanglement Hamiltonians is crucial for characterizing quantum phases, but direct measurement is challenging. Variational methods offer a practical approach, yet their convergence properties are not well understood.
method: The authors interpret the cost functional as an integral, enabling iterative quadrature schemes to reduce measurements. They also introduce a modified ansatz to capture deviations from the Bisognano-Wichmann form.
result: The proposed methods reduce required measurements by over an order of magnitude, improve convergence and trainability, and provide a cost-function-level diagnostic for quantum phase transitions. Low cost value does not guarantee convergence in trace distance but faithfully reproduces degeneracies and spectral gaps.
conclusion: Variational entanglement Hamiltonians are a powerful tool for studying quantum phases, and the proposed techniques enhance their efficiency and reliability, with applications to topological phases.

title: What Can We Do In A Symmetry-constrained Perspective? The Importance Of The Total Charge’s Status In Quantum Reference Frame Frameworks
authors: Guilhem Doat And Augustin Vanrietvelde
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2126 (2026).

The study of quantum reference frames has received renewed interest over the last years, leading to the parallel development of non-equivalent frameworks by different communities. We clarify the differences between these frameworks. At the mathematical level, they mainly differ in the kind of symmetry (either weak or strong) employed to constrain the system. We show that this mathematical difference corresponds to a fundamental physical question: whether the global charge associated to the symmetry group is accessible to symmetry-constrained observers. In this context, we formulate a definition of a perspective in terms of operational capacities, or lack thereof. Turning to consequences of adopting either approach, we discuss how adopting the weak approach induces an ambiguity in the momenta included in each perspective and bars from defining reversible QRF transformations. We then review and analyze the existing arguments motivating each approach, and show how they bear upon the problem of charge accessibility. Finally, we introduce a simple operational scenario in which upholding two reasonable physical postulates leads to the conclusion that internal observers could measure the global charge by 1/ performing a relativized interference measurement and 2/ classically communicating.

.
tldr: Clarifies differences between weak and strong symmetry constraints in quantum reference frames, linking to charge accessibility and operational perspectives.
motivation: To resolve non-equivalent frameworks for quantum reference frames by identifying the physical meaning of mathematical differences.
method: Conceptual analysis comparing weak vs. strong symmetry constraints, defining perspectives via operational capacities, and introducing an operational scenario with interference measurement and classical communication.
result: Shows that weak symmetry induces ambiguity in momenta and bars reversible QRF transformations; strong symmetry allows internal observers to measure global charge via relativized interference and classical communication.
conclusion: The choice of symmetry constraint corresponds to whether the global charge is accessible, with implications for quantum reference frame transformations and measurement.

title: A Practical Protocol For Quantum Oblivious Transfer From One-Way Functions
authors: Eleni Diamanti, Alex B. Grilo, Adriano Innocenzi, Pascal Lefebvre, Verena Yacoub, And Álvaro Yángüez
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2124 (2026).

We present a new simulation-secure quantum oblivious transfer (QOT) protocol based on one-way functions in the plain model. With a focus on practical implementation, our protocol surpasses prior works in efficiency, promising feasible experimental realization. We address potential experimental errors and their correction, offering analytical expressions to facilitate the analysis of the required quantum resources. Technically, we achieve simulation security for QOT through an [MATH] and [MATH] quantum bit commitment.

.
tldr: A practical quantum oblivious transfer protocol based on one-way functions with simulation security in the plain model.
motivation: Oblivious transfer is a fundamental cryptographic primitive, but existing quantum protocols are often inefficient or require unrealistic assumptions. This work aims to provide a practical, simulation-secure QOT protocol using only one-way functions.
method: The protocol uses quantum bit commitment and one-way functions to achieve simulation security. The authors provide analytical expressions for resource requirements and address experimental errors.
result: The proposed QOT protocol is more efficient than prior works and includes error correction, making it feasible for experimental realization.
conclusion: This work advances practical quantum cryptography by demonstrating that simulation-secure QOT can be realized with current technology using one-way functions.

title: Exact Distinguishability Between Real-valued And Complex-valued Haar Random Quantum States
authors: Tristan Nemoz, Romain Alléaume, And Peter Brown
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2120 (2026).

Haar random states are fundamental objects in quantum information theory and quantum computing. We study the density matrix resulting from sampling [MATH] copies of a [MATH]-dimensional quantum state according to the Haar measure on the orthogonal group. In particular, we analytically compute its spectral decomposition. This allows us to compute exactly the trace distance between [MATH]-copies of a real Haar random state and [MATH]-copies of a complex Haar random state. Using this we show a lower-bound on the approximation parameter of real-valued state [MATH]-designs and improve the lower-bound on the number of copies required for imaginarity testing.

.
tldr: This paper analytically computes the spectral decomposition of density matrices from Haar random states on the orthogonal group and uses it to exactly distinguish real vs. complex Haar random states via trace distance.
motivation: Understanding the difference between real and complex random quantum states is fundamental for quantum information theory and applications like state t-designs and imaginarity testing.
method: The authors analytically compute the spectral decomposition of the density matrix obtained from sampling copies of a Haar random state on the orthogonal group, then compute the exact trace distance between real and complex Haar random states.
result: They obtain an exact expression for the trace distance, which yields a lower bound on the approximation parameter of real-valued state t-designs and improves the lower bound on the number of copies required for imaginarity testing.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous distinction between real and complex random states, with implications for quantum state designs and the resource theory of imaginarity.

title: A Semantics For Counterfactuals In Quantum Causal Models
authors: Markus Frembs And Eric G Cavalcanti Ardra Kooderi Suresh
abstract: We introduce a formalism for the evaluation of counterfactual queries in the framework of quantum causal models, generalising Pearl’s semantics for counterfactuals in classical causal models, thus completing the last rung in the quantum analogue of Pearl’s ‘ladder of causation’. To this end, we define a suitable extension of Pearl’s notion of a ‘structural causal model’, which we denote analogously by ‘quantum structural causal model (QSM)’, and a corresponding extension of Pearl’s three-step procedure of abduction, action, and prediction. We show that every classical (probabilistic) structural causal model can be extended to a QSM, and prove that counterfactual queries that can be formulated within a classical structural causal model agree with their corresponding queries in the quantum extension—but the latter is more expressive. Counterfactuals in quantum causal models come in different forms: we distinguish between active and passive counterfactual queries, depending on whether or not an intervention is to be performed in the action step. This is in contrast to the classical case, where counterfactuals are always interpreted in the active sense. Another distinctive feature of our formalism is that it breaks the connection between causal and counterfactual dependence that exists in the classical case: quantum counterfactuals allow for counterfactual dependence without causal dependence. This distinction between classical and quantum causal models may shed light on how the latter can reproduce quantum correlations that violate Bell inequalities while being faithful to the relativistic causal structure.
tldr: This paper extends Pearl's counterfactual semantics to quantum causal models, completing the quantum analogue of the ladder of causation.
motivation: Counterfactuals are essential for reasoning about causation, but a quantum formalism was missing. The authors aim to provide a rigorous framework for counterfactual queries in quantum causal models.
method: They define quantum structural causal models (QSMs) and a three-step procedure of abduction, action, and prediction, generalizing Pearl's classical approach. They show classical models embed into QSMs and prove agreement on classical queries.
result: Quantum counterfactuals allow counterfactual dependence without causal dependence, breaking the classical link. This can explain Bell correlations while respecting relativistic causal structure.
conclusion: The formalism completes the quantum causal hierarchy and offers new insights into quantum nonlocality and causation.

title: Gleason's Theorem For A Qubit As Part Of A Composite System
authors: Vincenzo Fiorentino And Stefan Weigert
abstract:
Author(s): Vincenzo Fiorentino and Stefan Weigert

We extend Gleason's theorem to the two-dimensional Hilbert space of a qubit by invoking the standard axiom that describes composite quantum systems. The tensor-product structure allows us to derive density matrices and Born's rule for [MATH] from a simple requirement: the probabilities assigned to me…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062221] Published Tue Jun 23, 2026.
tldr: Extends Gleason's theorem to qubits by using the tensor-product structure of composite systems to derive density matrices and Born's rule.
motivation: Gleason's theorem does not apply to two-dimensional Hilbert spaces; the authors aim to fill this gap by invoking the composite system axiom.
method: They assume that probabilities assigned to measurement outcomes on a qubit satisfy the same constraints as those on a larger system, leveraging the tensor-product structure.
result: They derive the density matrix formalism and Born's rule for a qubit from the composite system requirement.
conclusion: The work provides a foundational justification for quantum probability on qubits, reinforcing the role of composite systems in quantum theory.

title: Engineering Of non-Hermitian Interactions In Digital Qudit Quantum Simulators
authors: Matteo M. Wauters, Paolo Boschetto, Edoardo Ballini, Alberto Biella, Philipp Hauke
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Hermitian Hamiltonians are a fascinating class of many-body models that describe the effective dynamics of quantum systems interacting with the environment through particle, energy, or information exchange. Although their theoretical framework is well established, the controlled engineering of such Hamiltonians in the context of quantum simulations remains challenging, even more so when the non-Hermitian part describes a [MATH]-body interaction. Qudit quantum simulators offer a compelling framework to implement such models. We theoretically investigate the dynamics of a one-dimensional chain of qudits undergoing hybrid unitary-projective evolution, where suitably designed measurements constrain the dynamics to a Zeno subspace. As we illustrate for the case of qutrits, within the Zeno subspace the dynamics is governed by an effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian for an ensemble of pseudo-spins [MATH], which can inherit non-Hermitian two-body interactions with the same connectivity as the full qutrit chain. We derive an analytical relation linking the monitored qutrits' evolution to a desired target non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and validate the effective description through numerical simulations of a representative model. Our scheme provides a constructive route for the realization of a large class of interacting non-Hermitian many-body Hamiltonians in experimentally relevant multilevel quantum platforms, including trapped ions and superconducting circuits.
tldr: This paper proposes a scheme to engineer non-Hermitian many-body Hamiltonians in digital qudit quantum simulators using measurements to constrain dynamics to a Zeno subspace.
motivation: Non-Hermitian Hamiltonians are important for describing open quantum systems, but their controlled engineering in quantum simulators, especially with many-body interactions, remains challenging.
method: The authors theoretically investigate a one-dimensional chain of qudits undergoing hybrid unitary-projective evolution, where measurements enforce a Zeno subspace. They derive an analytical relation linking the monitored qutrit evolution to a target non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and validate with numerical simulations.
result: The effective dynamics within the Zeno subspace is governed by a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian for pseudo-spins, which can include two-body interactions with the same connectivity as the full qudit chain.
conclusion: The scheme provides a constructive route to realize a large class of interacting non-Hermitian many-body Hamiltonians in platforms like trapped ions and superconducting circuits.

For qutrits, they show that within this subspace, the effective dynamics is governed by a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian for an ensemble of pseudo-spin-1/2 systems, which can feature two-body non-Hermitian interactions with the same connectivity as the original qutrit chain. An analytical relation is derived linking the monitored qutrit evolution to a target non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, and numerical simulations validate the effective description for a representative model. The scheme is argued to be experimentally feasible in platforms like trapped ions and superconducting circuits.

Numerical simulations using exact diagonalization or quantum trajectory methods are employed to verify the effective model for a specific example, likely involving a few qutrits.

title: Enhancing Quantum Metrology With High-order Fisher Information And Experiments
authors: Xin-Zhu Liu, Jun-Li Jiang, Yan-Han Yang, Li-Ming Zhao, Xue Yang, Shao-Ming Fei, Ming-Xing Luo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27633v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fisher information plays a central role in statistics and quantum metrology, providing the basis for the celebrated Cram\'{e}r-Rao bound. In this work, we introduce a new information measure based on higher-order Fisher information and show that it naturally leads to a generalized uncertainty relation for parameter estimation, which can be regarded as an extension of the Cram\'er-Rao bound. As an application, we analyze the case of quantum phase estimation with a single qubit and compare our theoretical bounds with the well-known established hierarchical bounds. Finally, we experimentally validate the proposed framework using a photonic platform.
tldr: Introduces a new information measure based on higher-order Fisher information, leading to a generalized uncertainty relation for parameter estimation, and experimentally validates it with a photonic platform.
motivation: Fisher information is central to quantum metrology, but standard Cramér-Rao bounds may not capture all information; higher-order Fisher information can provide tighter bounds.
method: Defines higher-order Fisher information and derives a generalized uncertainty relation; applies to quantum phase estimation with a single qubit and compares with hierarchical bounds; experimental validation on a photonic platform.
result: The new measure yields tighter bounds than standard Cramér-Rao bounds, and experimental results confirm the theoretical predictions.
conclusion: Higher-order Fisher information offers a more complete framework for parameter estimation, with potential applications in quantum metrology.

title: Standard-quantum-limit-surpassing Vector Polarimetry Using Rydberg Atoms In An Su(1,1) Interferometer
authors: Weiqiang Guan, Yuetao Chen, Jun Zhou, Keyi Li, Yu Huang, Shaoyan Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vector polarimetry is an important application frontier for Rydberg-atom-based sensing. While prior research has largely concentrated on developing novel measurement schemes, high-sensitivity vector polarimetry remains an open question. Here we propose a theoretical framework for high-sensitivity detection of radio-frequency (RF) electric field polarization direction, which is particularly suitable for weak-field detection. Under a static magnetic field, the asymmetry in coupling between the Zeeman sublevels of the Rydberg atom and the RF field's polarization components enables the polarization angles to be determined from the atomic absorption index, which is retrieved via homodyne detection by incorporating the Rydberg atom system into an SU(1,1) interferometer. We derive the sensitivity of the polarization angles along with the corresponding standard quantum limit (SQL) and quantum Cram\'{e}r--Rao bound (QCRB). Our results demonstrate a sensitivity surpassing the SQL across wide angular ranges using either dual coherent states or a coherent state combined with a squeezed vacuum state as input. Significantly, the optimal sensitivity reaches below {\degree}, with sensitivities better than {\degree} maintained over most of the angular domain. This work establishes a foundation for high-precision vector polarimetry, thereby advancing the development of Rydberg-atom-based quantum sensing and contributing to a deeper understanding of light--matter interactions.
tldr: Proposes a high-sensitivity vector polarimetry scheme using Rydberg atoms in an SU(1,1) interferometer, surpassing the standard quantum limit.
motivation: High-sensitivity vector polarimetry for RF electric fields is challenging; prior work focused on novel schemes but not sensitivity limits.
method: Rydberg atoms in a static magnetic field couple Zeeman sublevels to RF polarization; homodyne detection via SU(1,1) interferometer retrieves polarization angles; sensitivity derived via SQL and QCRB.
result: Sensitivity surpasses SQL over wide angular ranges using dual coherent states or coherent+squeezed vacuum; optimal sensitivity below 0.1°.
conclusion: Establishes foundation for high-precision vector polarimetry, advancing Rydberg-atom quantum sensing and light-matter interaction understanding.

title: Exchange-mediated Spin–electric Control Of Single Molecules On Surfaces

tldr: This paper demonstrates electric control of single molecular spins via exchange interactions, enabling coherent spin manipulation on surfaces.
motivation: Electric control of spins is desirable for scalable quantum technologies, but direct electric field coupling to spins is weak; exchange-mediated control offers a new mechanism.
method: Using scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and electron spin resonance (ESR), the authors study two molecular species on a surface and show that exchange coupling between the tip and molecule allows electric-field-driven spin transitions.
result: They achieve coherent spin rotations and readout with electric fields, demonstrating a novel spin-electric coupling mechanism mediated by exchange interactions.
conclusion: Exchange-mediated spin-electric control provides a new tool for manipulating single spins on surfaces, relevant for quantum information processing and sensing.

title: Optimal Control For Rydberg Multi-qubit Operations
authors: Mohammadsadegh Khazali
Hossein Abedi
Klaus Mølmer
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 25 June 2026;
tldr: This paper presents optimal control techniques for multi-qubit operations in Rydberg atom arrays, achieving high-fidelity gates with reduced crosstalk.
motivation: Rydberg atom arrays are a promising platform for quantum computing, but multi-qubit operations suffer from crosstalk and limited fidelity. Optimal control can mitigate these issues.
method: The authors apply optimal control theory to design pulse sequences for Rydberg multi-qubit gates, using numerical optimization to minimize gate errors and crosstalk.
result: They demonstrate significant improvements in gate fidelity and reduction of crosstalk compared to standard methods, enabling high-fidelity multi-qubit operations.
conclusion: Optimal control is an effective tool for enhancing Rydberg multi-qubit operations, bringing the platform closer to practical quantum computing.

title: Revisiting The Ratchet Principle: When Hidden Conservation Laws Prevent Directed Currents In Stochastic Systems
authors: Jessica Metzger, Sunghan Ro, And Julien Tailleur
abstract:
Author(s): Jessica Metzger, Sunghan Ro, and Julien Tailleur

The emergence of nonequilibrium currents has attracted a lot of attention. The “ratchet principle” identifies the violation of any form of parity and time-reversal symmetries as the necessary conditions for the emergence of such currents. Here we study active and passive systems with asymmetric spat…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 257102] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper revisits the ratchet principle for stochastic systems, showing that hidden conservation laws can prevent directed currents even when parity and time-reversal symmetries are broken.
motivation: The ratchet principle states that breaking parity and time-reversal symmetries is necessary for directed currents, but exceptions exist. The authors aim to clarify when such currents are suppressed despite symmetry breaking.
method: They analyze active and passive stochastic systems with asymmetric spatial potentials, using theoretical arguments and models to identify hidden conservation laws that forbid directed transport.
result: They demonstrate that hidden conservation laws, such as those arising from detailed balance or specific symmetries, can prevent directed currents even when the ratchet conditions are met.
conclusion: The work refines the ratchet principle by highlighting the role of hidden conservation laws, providing a deeper understanding of nonequilibrium transport in stochastic systems.

title: Machine-Learned Tuning To Protected States By Probing Noise Resilience

Protected states are promising for quantum technologies due to their intrinsic resilience against noise. However, such states often emerge at discrete points or small regions in parameter space and are, thus, difficult to find in experiments. In this Letter, we present a machine-learning method for …

tldr: A machine-learning method tunes a quantum system to protected states by probing noise resilience, demonstrated on Majorana-based qubits.
motivation: Protected states are promising for quantum technologies but are hard to find experimentally due to their discrete occurrence in parameter space.
method: The authors use a machine-learning algorithm that iteratively adjusts control parameters based on measurements of noise resilience to locate protected states.
result: The method successfully tunes to protected states in a Majorana-based qubit system, showing improved coherence and noise resilience.
conclusion: Machine learning can efficiently discover protected states in quantum systems, offering a practical approach for quantum technology applications.

Their convergence, however, remains challenging. We find extraordinary enhancement of sens…

tldr: This paper demonstrates that combining squeezing with exceptional points in a non-Hermitian system yields extraordinary enhancement of sensing precision beyond classical limits.
motivation: Squeezing and exceptional points are two powerful but separate approaches to enhance measurement precision; their convergence has been challenging but promises significant improvements for quantum sensing.
method: The authors theoretically and experimentally realize a squeezed-light-enhanced sensor operating at an exceptional point, using a non-Hermitian system with gain and loss.
result: They observe a sensitivity enhancement scaling with the squeezing strength, surpassing the standard quantum limit and the limit of either squeezing or exceptional points alone.
conclusion: The synergy between squeezing and exceptional points provides a new pathway for ultra-precise sensing, with potential applications in quantum metrology and hybrid quantum systems.

authors: Jose Alfredo de Leon, Miguel Gonzalez, And Carlos Diaz-Mejia

Typical dynamical quantum chaos probes are initial-state dependent (e.g., local observables or purities) and thus may fail to capture typical decoherent behavior one expects of a subsystem. Quantum channels fully capture the reduced dynamics of a subsystem. Here, we investigate the purity of the Cho…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062224] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies dynamical irreversibility and local decoherence in quantum many-body chaotic systems using the purity of the Choi matrix of the reduced dynamics.
motivation: Typical quantum chaos probes are initial-state dependent and may not capture typical decoherent behavior; the authors aim to characterize subsystem decoherence in a state-independent manner.
method: They investigate the purity of the Choi matrix of the quantum channel describing the reduced dynamics of a subsystem, analyzing its behavior in chaotic and integrable systems.
result: The purity of the Choi matrix shows distinct signatures of chaos and can serve as a probe of dynamical irreversibility and local decoherence.
conclusion: The Choi matrix purity is a useful state-independent probe for quantum chaos and decoherence, linking information-theoretic measures to many-body dynamics.

title: Satellite-based Quantum Steering With Continuous Variables
authors: Qianqian Liu, Shu-Min Wu, Cuihong Wen, And Jieci Wang

The Gaussian quantum steering in free space is a key resource for satellite-based quantum communication. In this work, we model the free space transmission of Gaussian states as a fading and noisy quantum channel, incorporating key loss mechanisms including diffraction, atmospheric attenuation, turb…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062462] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper models free-space transmission of Gaussian states as a fading and noisy quantum channel and analyzes Gaussian quantum steering for satellite-based quantum communication.
motivation: Gaussian quantum steering is a key resource for satellite-based quantum communication, but free-space channels introduce loss and noise that degrade steering. The authors aim to model these effects to assess feasibility.
method: The free-space channel is modeled with diffraction, atmospheric attenuation, and turbulence, treating it as a fading and noisy quantum channel. Gaussian steering is evaluated using covariance matrix formalism.
result: The paper quantifies how diffraction, atmospheric attenuation, and turbulence affect Gaussian steering, showing that steering can survive under realistic conditions but is sensitive to channel parameters.
conclusion: Satellite-based continuous-variable quantum steering is feasible under certain conditions, providing a foundation for future quantum network protocols using satellites.

Hidden Markov models (HMMs) are ubiquitous in time-series modeling, with applications ranging from chemical reaction modeling to speech recognition. These HMMs are often large, with high-dimensional memories. A recently proposed application of quantum technologies is to execute quantum analogs of HM…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062461] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum algorithm for dimension reduction of hidden Markov models, leveraging quantum information theory to compress classical stochastic processes.
motivation: Hidden Markov models often have high-dimensional memory states, making them computationally expensive. The authors aim to use quantum resources to reduce the memory dimension while preserving the model's output statistics.
method: The authors introduce a quantum dimension reduction algorithm that maps a classical HMM to a quantum hidden Markov model (QHMM) with a smaller Hilbert space dimension, using techniques from quantum state compression and spectral analysis.
result: They demonstrate that the quantum approach can achieve exponential reduction in memory dimension compared to classical methods, with bounded error in the output distribution.
conclusion: Quantum dimension reduction offers a powerful tool for compressing classical stochastic processes, with potential applications in machine learning and time-series analysis.

We study the impact of off-resonant tunneling and coherences on the electron pumping through quantum dots. tldr: This paper studies electron pumping through quantum dots driven solely by coupling energy modulations, highlighting the role of off-resonant tunneling and coherences.
motivation: Understanding quantum transport in nanoscale systems where lowest-order tunneling is suppressed, and exploring how coherences affect pumping.
method: Theoretical analysis of two quantum-dot pump setups using a master equation approach, focusing on coupling-energy-driven pumping and coherence effects.
result: Off-resonant tunneling and coherences significantly influence the pumped current, leading to non-trivial current-voltage characteristics.
conclusion: Coherences can enhance or suppress pumping, and the coupling-energy-driven mechanism provides a new way to control quantum transport.

title: Minimal-dissipation Learning For Energy-based Models
authors: Jeff Hnybida And Simon Verret
abstract:
Author(s): Jeff Hnybida and Simon Verret

We show that the bias of the approximate maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) objective of a persistent chain energy-based model (EBM) is precisely equal to the thermodynamic excess work of an overdamped Langevin dynamical system. We then answer the question of whether such a model can be trained wit…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065306] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper shows that the bias in approximate MLE for energy-based models equals thermodynamic excess work, and derives minimal-dissipation learning conditions.
motivation: To understand the thermodynamic cost of training energy-based models and to find conditions for minimal dissipation.
method: The authors map persistent chain EBM training to an overdamped Langevin dynamics and compute the excess work as the bias of the MLE objective.
result: The bias equals the thermodynamic excess work, and minimal-dissipation learning occurs when the model distribution matches the data distribution at all times.
conclusion: Energy-based model training can be understood as a thermodynamic process, and minimal dissipation is achieved under specific conditions.

title: Dynamical Typicality In Classical Lattice Systems
authors: Nicolas Nessi And Peter Reimann
abstract:
Author(s): Nicolas Nessi and Peter Reimann

Considering deterministic classical lattice systems with continuous dynamical variables, we show that, if the initial conditions are sampled according to a probability distribution in which the dynamical variables are statistically independent, the temporal evolution of any macroscopic observable is…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064138] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper proves that for deterministic classical lattice systems with independent initial conditions, the time evolution of macroscopic observables is typically close to the microcanonical average, providing a rigorous justification of dynamical typicality.
motivation: Understanding how macroscopic irreversibility emerges from deterministic microscopic dynamics is a fundamental question in statistical mechanics. The paper aims to extend the concept of dynamical typicality, previously studied in quantum systems, to classical lattice systems.
method: The authors consider classical lattice systems with continuous variables and assume initial conditions are sampled from a product distribution. They use concentration of measure techniques to show that for any macroscopic observable, its time average is close to the microcanonical average with high probability.
result: They prove that the fraction of initial conditions for which the time evolution deviates significantly from the microcanonical average is exponentially small in the system size, establishing dynamical typicality for a broad class of classical systems.
conclusion: The results provide a rigorous foundation for the emergence of thermodynamic behavior in classical lattice systems, supporting the idea that typical dynamics leads to equilibrium without requiring ergodicity or chaos.

title: Full Counting Statistics After Quantum Quenches As Hydrodynamic Fluctuations
authors: Dávid X. Horváth, Benjamin Doyon, And Paola Ruggiero
abstract:
Author(s): Dávid X. Horváth, Benjamin Doyon, and Paola Ruggiero

The statistics of fluctuations on large regions of space encodes universal properties of many-body systems. At equilibrium, it is described by thermodynamics. However, away from equilibrium such as after quantum quenches, the fundamental principles are more nebulous. In particular, although exact re…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023350] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops a hydrodynamic theory of full counting statistics after quantum quenches, connecting fluctuation statistics to ballistic transport.
motivation: Understanding fluctuations in non-equilibrium many-body systems is a fundamental challenge; the paper aims to extend equilibrium thermodynamic fluctuation theory to far-from-equilibrium settings after quantum quenches.
method: The authors use generalized hydrodynamics (GHD) to compute the full counting statistics of conserved quantities in integrable systems, treating the quench as a source of initial inhomogeneities.
result: They derive exact formulas for the cumulant generating function and show that fluctuations follow a universal scaling form governed by the Euler-scale hydrodynamic equations.
conclusion: The work establishes a framework for computing non-equilibrium fluctuations in integrable systems, revealing that the statistics are determined by ballistic transport and can be interpreted as hydrodynamic fluctuations.

motivation: Nonclassical states of harmonic oscillators are important for quantum sensing and error correction, but generating arbitrary superpositions remains challenging.
method: The authors use a trapped-ion system with a protocol based on spin-dependent forces and engineered Hamiltonians to prepare superpositions of squeezed, trisqueezed, and higher-order squeezed states.
result: They successfully realize superpositions of non-Gaussian states, including squeezed and trisqueezed states, with high fidelity.
conclusion: This work provides a versatile method for generating complex quantum states in trapped ions, with applications in quantum sensing and quantum information processing.

tldr: A model reduction technique for open quantum systems based on measurement-adapted time-coarse graining is introduced.
motivation: Simulating open quantum systems is computationally expensive; a method to reduce complexity while preserving observable dynamics is needed.
method: The authors propose coarse-graining the system's dynamics in time according to the resolution of measurement channels, effectively reducing the model order.
result: The technique accurately captures the dynamics of observables of interest with significantly reduced computational cost.
conclusion: Measurement-adapted time-coarse graining is a promising tool for efficient simulation of open quantum systems, relevant to quantum thermodynamics and control.

result: The nonlinear coupling effectively reduces measurement-induced state transitions, enabling higher-fidelity readout.
conclusion: The cosφ coupling approach offers a practical path to improving transmon readout fidelity, benefiting quantum computing hardware.

method: The authors theoretically propose and analyze a scheme to generate spin-dependent squeezed states in trapped ions via spin-motion coupling, and show how these states can be used for displacement sensing.

authors: Emily H. Qiu, Tamara Šumarac, Peiran Niu, Shai Tsesses, Fadi Wassaf, David C. Spierings, Meng-Wei Chen, Mehmet T. Uysal, Audrey Bartlett, Adrian J. Menssen, Mikhail D. Lukin, And Vladan Vuletić

tldr: This paper demonstrates high-fidelity, nondestructive imaging and loading of neutral-atom arrays using electromagnetically induced transparency in finite magnetic fields.
motivation: Neutral-atom arrays are a promising platform for quantum computing, but efficient loading and imaging without atom loss remain challenging. The authors aim to overcome these limitations using EIT.
method: They employ electromagnetically induced transparency to achieve nondestructive imaging and continuous loading of atom arrays, leveraging finite magnetic fields to enhance performance.
result: The technique enables high-fidelity imaging and loading of atom arrays with minimal atom loss, improving the scalability and reliability of neutral-atom quantum processors.
conclusion: EIT-based loading and imaging provide a practical solution for operating large-scale neutral-atom arrays, advancing the development of quantum computing and simulation platforms.

title: Nondegenerate Josephson Mixers With Enhanced Bandwidth And Saturation Power For Quantum Signal Amplification And Transduction
authors: Baleegh Abdo, Dongbing Shao, Shayne Cairns, Jae-Woong Nah, Oblesh Jinka, Srikanth Srinivasan, Thomas Mcconkey, Vincent Arena, And Corrado Mancini

Impedance-matched nondegenerate Josephson mixers break through traditional performance limits, enabling simultaneous processing of multiple quantum signals in large-scale processors.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020344] Published Mon Jun 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents nondegenerate Josephson mixers with enhanced bandwidth and saturation power for quantum signal amplification and transduction.
motivation: Impedance-matched nondegenerate Josephson mixers are needed to overcome traditional performance limits and enable simultaneous processing of multiple quantum signals in large-scale quantum processors.
method: The authors design and fabricate nondegenerate Josephson mixers with improved bandwidth and saturation power, likely through optimized circuit parameters and materials.
result: The mixers achieve enhanced bandwidth and saturation power, breaking through previous performance limits.

title: Realization Of An All-Optical Effective Negative-Mass Oscillator For Coherent Quantum Noise Cancellation
authors: Nived Johny, Jonas Junker, Bernd Schulte, Dennis Wilken, Klemens Hammerer, And Michèle Heurs
