Ultrafast photoexcitation in /3Ca1/3MnO3 generates a long-lived hidden phase with unique polaronic and phononic excitations that do not exist under standard equilibrium conditions.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021018] Published Thu Apr 23, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies photoinduced hidden phases and excitations in magnetoresistive manganites using ultrafast spectroscopy.
motivation: To understand the non-equilibrium dynamics and hidden phases in strongly correlated electron systems.
method: Ultrafast photoexcitation and resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) to probe excitations.
result: Discovery of a long-lived hidden phase with unique polaronic and phononic excitations not present in equilibrium.
conclusion: Photoexcitation can induce metastable hidden phases with distinct properties in manganites.

title: Entropy Of Strongly Correlated Electrons In A Partially Filled Landau Level
authors: Alexandre Assouline, Taige Wang, Heun Mo Yoo, Ruihua Fan, Fangyuan Yang, Ruining Zhang, Takashi Taniguchi, Kenji Watanabe, Michael P. Zaletel, And Andrea F. Young
abstract:
Author(s): Alexandre Assouline, Taige Wang, Heun Mo Yoo, Ruihua Fan, Fangyuan Yang, Ruining Zhang, Takashi Taniguchi, Kenji Watanabe, Michael P. Zaletel, and Andrea F. Young

Entropy measurements in partially filled Landau levels reveal the successive freezing of spin and motional degrees of freedom, reaching sensitivities that constrain the isolation of topological entropy in non-Abelian quantum phases.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021016] Published Fri Apr 17, 2026.
tldr: Entropy measurements in partially filled Landau levels reveal freezing of spin and motional degrees of freedom, with sensitivity to constrain topological entropy in non-Abelian phases.
motivation: To measure entropy in strongly correlated electron systems in the quantum Hall regime, probing the freezing of degrees of freedom and topological entropy.
method: Experimental entropy measurements using a graphene-based device in a partially filled Landau level, with sensitivity to distinguish spin and motional entropy.
result: Observed successive freezing of spin and motional degrees of freedom, achieving sensitivity that could constrain topological entropy in non-Abelian quantum phases.
conclusion: The measurements provide a thermodynamic probe of quantum Hall states, but the paper focuses on condensed matter physics without direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics of information processing.

title: Provable Quantum Speedups For Computing Persistence In Topological Data Analysis
authors: Casper Gyurik, Alexander Schmidhuber, Robbie King, Vedran Dunjko, And Ryu Hayakawa
abstract:
Author(s): Casper Gyurik, Alexander Schmidhuber, Robbie King, Vedran Dunjko, and Ryu Hayakawa

A quantum algorithm achieving exponential speedup for a topological data analysis problem is proposed, potentially driving new practical applications in quantum computing.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020361] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum algorithm for computing persistence in topological data analysis, claiming exponential speedup.
motivation: Topological data analysis is a classical machine learning technique; quantum speedups could enable analysis of larger datasets.
method: The authors design a quantum algorithm that leverages quantum linear algebra and topological invariants to compute persistence diagrams.
result: They prove an exponential speedup over classical algorithms for certain instances of persistence computation.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a potential quantum advantage in a practical data analysis task, but the connection to quantum information theory or thermodynamics is weak.

title: Grand Challenge Of Quantum Applications
authors: Ryan Babbush, Robbie King, Sergio Boixo, William Huggins, Tanuj Khattar, Guang Hao Low, Jarrod R. Mcclean, Thomas O’brien, And Nicholas C. Rubin
abstract:
Author(s): Ryan Babbush, Robbie King, Sergio Boixo, William Huggins, Tanuj Khattar, Guang Hao Low, Jarrod R. McClean, Thomas O’Brien, and Nicholas C. Rubin

A proposed five-stage framework outlines the path to useful quantum computing, detailing the scientific milestones required to bridge the gap between theory and real-world utility.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020101] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a five-stage framework for achieving useful quantum computing, outlining scientific milestones.
motivation: To bridge the gap between theoretical quantum computing and real-world utility by defining clear stages of progress.
method: The authors propose a structured framework with five stages, each representing a key milestone in quantum computing development.
result: A five-stage roadmap is presented, detailing the necessary scientific and technological advancements.
conclusion: The framework provides a high-level vision for the quantum computing community to focus efforts on achieving practical quantum advantage.

title: Photon Catalysis For General Multimode Multi-Photon Quantum State Preparation
authors: Andrei Aralov, Émilie Gillet, Viet Nguyen, Andrea Cosentino, Mattia Walschaers, And Massimo Frigerio
abstract:
Author(s): Andrei Aralov, Émilie Gillet, Viet Nguyen, Andrea Cosentino, Mattia Walschaers, and Massimo Frigerio

Using a procedure based on symmetric tensor decomposition, every photonic state can be prepared with realistic experimental tools and a predictable number of steps.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020323] Published Wed May 06, 2026.
tldr: A method for preparing arbitrary multimode multi-photon states using symmetric tensor decomposition and realistic experimental tools.
motivation: General photonic state preparation is important for quantum information processing, but existing methods are limited to specific states or require complex resources.
method: The authors propose a procedure based on symmetric tensor decomposition to decompose any photonic state into a sequence of operations achievable with current experimental platforms.
result: They show that any multimode multi-photon state can be prepared with a predictable number of steps using realistic tools.
conclusion: This provides a universal and efficient approach to photonic state preparation, potentially enabling new quantum information protocols.

title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge and recent discoveries in 2D magnetism.
method: Review of experimental and theoretical studies on 2D van der Waals magnetic materials.
result: The field encompasses ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, topology, quantum dynamics, and spintronics.
conclusion: 2D van der Waals magnets are a rapidly evolving field with potential for new physics and applications.

title: Radiation Forces And Torques In Optics And Acoustics
authors: Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, And Konstantin Y. Bliokh
abstract:
Author(s): Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, and Konstantin Y. Bliokh

This review presents a unified perspective of how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in optical and acoustic wave fields induce forces and torques on particles—a topic that has captivated researchers for centuries. Applications discussed include trapping and manipulation of atoms and nanoparticles by light, sorting of biological cells by the combination of acoustics and microfluidics, and pulling forces that draw particles against the direction of wave propagation.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025002] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: This review unifies the description of radiation forces and torques in optical and acoustic fields, focusing on momentum and spin densities.
motivation: Understanding how wave fields exert forces and torques on particles is fundamental for applications like optical trapping and acoustic manipulation.
method: The authors present a unified theoretical framework based on local energy, momentum, and spin densities in optical and acoustic waves.
result: They show that both optical and acoustic fields induce similar force and torque effects, enabling applications such as particle trapping, sorting, and pulling.
conclusion: The unified perspective highlights common principles across optics and acoustics, guiding future work in wave-matter interactions.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on electronic states and many-body phenomena arising from the kagome lattice geometry.
motivation: To understand the exotic electronic states in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and topological flat bands.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, analyzing electronic structure and correlation effects.
result: Identifies key phenomena including topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, and unconventional superconductivity.
conclusion: Kagome metals host a rich variety of correlated and topological electronic phases, offering a platform for studying strong correlations and frustration.

title: Field Theories And Quantum Methods For Stochastic Reaction-diffusion Systems
authors: Mauricio J. Del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, And Wout Merbis
abstract:
Author(s): Mauricio J. del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, and Wout Merbis

The exchange of energy and molecules in a living cell, the spread of opinions through a society, and the flow of traffic in a crowded city are very different phenomena, yet they are all examples of complex systems composed of many agents that interact with each other and exchange energy or particles with the environment. These systems can be modeled as stochastic reaction-diffusion systems. In this pedagogical review, the authors apply powerful field-theoretic methods to these systems, unifying diverse approaches under a single framework. The methods are useful for handling chemical systems but also have applications in a wide range of areas such as ecology and epidemiology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015001] Published Thu Jan 22, 2026.
tldr: A pedagogical review applying field-theoretic methods to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems in biology, ecology, and epidemiology.
motivation: To unify diverse approaches for modeling complex systems with many interacting agents, such as chemical reactions, population dynamics, and opinion spread.
method: The authors use field-theoretic techniques, including path integrals and Doi-Peliti formalism, to derive and solve stochastic reaction-diffusion equations.
result: The review demonstrates how field theories provide a systematic framework for analyzing fluctuations and correlations in reaction-diffusion systems.
conclusion: Field-theoretic methods are powerful tools for stochastic reaction-diffusion systems, with broad applicability beyond physics.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation.
motivation: Spin glasses are a model system for complex disordered systems, and understanding their dynamics has broad applications.
method: The review synthesizes experimental results, theoretical developments, and large-scale simulations.
result: Highlights the synergy between experiment, theory, and simulation in advancing the field.
conclusion: Spin-glass dynamics remain a rich area for future research, with opportunities for further integration of approaches.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on candidate materials and topological properties.
motivation: To provide an overview of theoretical and experimental progress in Kitaev spin liquids, which are a type of quantum spin liquid with potential applications in topological quantum computing.
method: The paper reviews theoretical models (Kitaev honeycomb model) and experimental realizations in materials, highlighting chiral edge modes and other topological features.
result: The review summarizes key candidate materials and their properties, emphasizing the broad topological phenomena observed.
conclusion: Kitaev spin liquids are a rich field with many open questions, and the review provides essential insights for researchers.

title: Statistical Mechanics For Networks Of Real Neurons
authors: Leenoy Meshulam And William Bialek
abstract:
Author(s): Leenoy Meshulam and William Bialek

Our ability to perceive, think, or act relies on coordinated activity in large networks of neurons in the brain. This review examines recent progress in connecting ideas from statistical physics, such as maximum entropy methods and the renormalization group, to quantitative experiments that record the electrical activity of thousands of neurons simultaneously. This quantitative bridge between the new data and statistical physics models uncovers new, quantitatively reproducible behaviors and makes clear that abstract theoretical principles in studies of the brain can have the level of predictive power that we expect in other areas of physics.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045002] Published Thu Nov 06, 2025.
tldr: This review applies statistical physics methods like maximum entropy and renormalization group to analyze neural network activity in the brain.
motivation: Understanding how large networks of neurons coordinate activity to enable perception, thought, and action is a fundamental challenge in neuroscience.
method: The authors review recent progress in connecting maximum entropy models and renormalization group techniques to quantitative recordings of thousands of neurons.
result: These statistical physics approaches uncover new, quantitatively reproducible behaviors in neural activity, demonstrating predictive power comparable to other areas of physics.
conclusion: Statistical mechanics provides a powerful framework for analyzing neural network data, bridging theory and experiment in neuroscience.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, with applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: Internal conversion is a key nonradiative process in photophysics, and understanding its theoretical underpinnings is important for applications like photonics and energy harvesting.
method: The paper reviews various theoretical models describing internal conversion, covering all facets of the nonradiative mechanism.
result: The review presents an outlook on how these models can be incorporated into studies relevant to applications.
conclusion: Theoretical methods for internal conversion are well-developed and can be applied to practical photonic and energy harvesting systems.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews quantum properties and functionalities of magnetic skyrmions, focusing on their topological nature and potential applications.
motivation: Magnetic skyrmions are promising for spintronic devices, but their quantum aspects are less explored; this review aims to bridge that gap.
method: The paper surveys theoretical and experimental work on skyrmion formation, quantum interactions, and quantum features of skyrmions themselves.
result: It highlights quantum effects such as tunneling, superposition, and entanglement in skyrmion systems, and discusses their potential for quantum information processing.
conclusion: Skyrmions exhibit rich quantum behavior that could be harnessed for future technologies, but the field is still nascent.

title: Spin-dependent Exotic Interactions
authors: Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, And Dmitry Budker
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and Dmitry Budker

This review presents a comprehensive summary of theoretical investigations and experimental searches for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model. These interactions may be mediated by various types of exotic bosons, and their existence and properties may, in turn, explain the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The described experiments also probe the discrete fundamental symmetries of nature.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025005] Published Tue Jun 24, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the standard model, including their potential connection to dark matter and dark energy.
motivation: To understand possible new physics beyond the standard model, particularly spin-dependent forces mediated by exotic bosons that could explain dark matter and dark energy.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks for spin-dependent interactions and surveys experimental techniques used to search for such interactions, including precision measurements and astrophysical observations.
result: The review summarizes current constraints on various spin-dependent interaction parameters and highlights the most promising experimental approaches.
conclusion: Spin-dependent exotic interactions remain an active area of research with potential implications for fundamental physics, but no definitive evidence has been found yet.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining the violations by examining underlying assumptions.
motivation: Classical thermodynamic bounds are often assumed to be fundamental, but some measurements exceed them; understanding why clarifies the limits of thermodynamics and enables design of materials with extreme properties.
method: The paper surveys a wide variety of materials and phenomena where measured properties exceed classical bounds, and analyzes which assumptions (e.g., equilibrium, linear response) are violated in each case.
result: It identifies that violations occur because measurements are made in ways that violate assumptions behind the bounds, and shows how materials can be designed to exploit these violations.
conclusion: The apparent violations do not contradict thermodynamics but rather highlight the importance of assumptions; this understanding can guide development of materials with enhanced properties.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews experimental and theoretical implementations of fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems for simulating quantum many-body physics.
motivation: To explore quantum many-body phenomena in nonstandard geometries that are difficult to realize in conventional settings, such as topology and gravity analogs.
method: The paper surveys various platforms (cold atoms, photonics, electronic systems) and techniques for engineering synthetic lattices with fractal, curved, or higher-dimensional geometries.
result: It provides a comprehensive overview of current capabilities and theoretical frameworks for simulating exotic geometries, highlighting key experimental achievements and open challenges.
conclusion: Synthetic quantum matter in nonstandard geometries offers a powerful tool for studying fundamental physics, but the field is still developing with many opportunities for future work.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: A review of self-alignment in polar active matter, covering single-particle and collective behaviors.
motivation: To unify the understanding of self-alignment in active systems and highlight its potential for biology, smart materials, and robotics.
method: Review of existing models and experimental observations, presenting a unified mathematical and conceptual framework.
result: Self-alignment enables novel behaviors such as orbiting in harmonic traps and synchronized motion in dense assemblies.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a fundamental property that reshapes motion in active systems, with broad implications for applications.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: A review of experimental and theoretical efforts to probe gravity using massive quantum systems, focusing on decoherence and entanglement mediated by gravity.
motivation: Classical gravity is the least precisely tested fundamental force, and quantum probes may reveal its quantum nature.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks (e.g., decoherence models, entanglement tests) and experimental platforms (e.g., matter-wave interferometry, optomechanics) for testing gravity with massive quantum systems.
result: Current experiments are approaching the sensitivity needed to test whether gravity induces decoherence or entanglement, but no definitive results have been obtained yet.
conclusion: Massive quantum systems offer a promising avenue to study the interplay between quantum mechanics and gravity, but further theoretical and experimental advances are required.

title: Qubit Operations Using A Modular Optical System Engineered With PyOpticL: A code-to-CAD Optical Layout Tool
authors: Jacob Myers, Christopher Caron, Nishat Helaly, Zhenyu Wei, Justin Oh, Zack Gotobed, Kotaro Yabe, And Robert J. Niffenegger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2135 (2026).

Complex optical design is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and therefore abstraction of subsystems at the circuit level. This limits multiple fields that require complex optics systems, including quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions, because their optical systems are not scalable. We present an open-source Python library for optical layout (PyOpticL) which uses beam-path simulation and dynamic beam-path routing for quick and easy optical layout by placing optical elements along the beam path without a priori specification, enabling adaptive, path-based layouts with automatic routing and connectivity. We use PyOpticL to create modular `drop-in' optical baseplates for common optical subsystems used in atomic and molecular optics (AMO) experiments including laser sources, frequency and intensity modulation, and locking to an atomic reference for stabilization. We demonstrate this minimal working example of a dynamic full laser system for strontium trapped ions by using it for laser cooling, qubit state detection, and over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates. This enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems leveraging modular baseplates, as they can be used for any wavelength in the system and enables scaling up the underlying optical systems for quantum computers. This new open-source hardware and software code-to-CAD library seeks to foster open-source collaborative hardware and systems design across numerous fields of research including AMO physics and quantum computing with neutral atoms and trapped ions.

.
tldr: This paper presents PyOpticL, an open-source Python library for modular optical system design, and demonstrates its use for trapped-ion qubit operations.
motivation: Complex optical design in quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and scalability.
method: The authors developed PyOpticL, a code-to-CAD optical layout tool that uses beam-path simulation and dynamic routing to enable adaptive, path-based layouts. They created modular drop-in optical baseplates for common subsystems and demonstrated a full laser system for strontium trapped ions.
result: The system achieved over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates and enabled laser cooling and qubit state detection using 3D-printed baseplates.
conclusion: PyOpticL enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems, fostering open-source collaborative hardware design for quantum computing and AMO physics.

title: Bosonic Content Of Three-fermion Highest-spin States
authors: Jerzy Cioslowski, Krzysztof Strasburger, And Denis K. Sunko
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2121 (2026).

A rigorous characterization of the information content of any highest-spin three-fermion wave function is presented. It is based upon a formal decomposition of the wave function into a finite set of fixed invariants, called shapes, whose sole purpose is to satisfy the Pauli principle, and a variable part, constituting the bosonic excitations of these invariants, that provides its physical content. As an example, this decomposition is applied to a benchmark-quality approximate wave function of the lowest-energy quartet electronic state of the lithium atom. This wave function, which comprises hundreds of basis functions, is reduced to eleven shape blocks, only five of which are numerically significant. Such a compact characterization is a generic example of the appearance of superselection rules in configuration space, and provides a qualitative aid in the search for robust few-particle entangled states.

.
tldr: This paper decomposes three-fermion highest-spin wave functions into fixed invariants (shapes) and bosonic excitations, applied to the lithium atom.
motivation: To characterize the information content of fermionic wave functions and identify robust few-particle entangled states.
method: Formal decomposition of the wave function into shapes (satisfying Pauli principle) and bosonic excitations; applied to a benchmark lithium wave function.
result: The wave function reduces to eleven shape blocks, only five numerically significant, demonstrating superselection rules in configuration space.
conclusion: The compact characterization aids in searching for robust few-particle entangled states.

title: Classical Field Simulation Of Vortex Lattice Melting In A Two-dimensional Fast Rotating Bose Gas
authors: Sálvio J Bereta, Lucas Madeira, Mônica A Caracanhas, Hélène Perrin And Romain Dubessy
abstract: We present a classical field simulation study of the thermal melting of a two-dimensional (2D) vortex lattice in a rotating Bose gas, focusing on the role of finite-size effects on the melting temperature. This work constitutes a numerical continuation of the recent experimental investigation reported in (Sharma 2024 Phys. Rev. Lett.133 143401), which addressed the thermal melting of a vortex lattice in a quasi-2D Bose gas. Using the stochastic projected Gross–Pitaevskii equation in a harmonic plus quartic trap, we simulate the finite-temperature equilibrium state and extract vortex configurations from density snapshots. Clear signatures of the two-step Kosterlitz–Thouless–Halperin–Nelson–Young melting scenario are identified. Our simulations enable a detailed characterization of the crystalline, hexatic, and liquid phases through correlation functions quantifying the translational and orientational order and through defect statistics. Finite-size effects are shown to play a crucial role at lower rotation frequencies, affecting the proliferation of lattice defects.
tldr: This paper simulates vortex lattice melting in a rotating Bose gas using classical field methods, focusing on finite-size effects.
motivation: To understand the thermal melting of vortex lattices in two-dimensional Bose gases, which is a fundamental many-body physics problem, and to complement recent experimental observations.
method: Uses the stochastic projected Gross–Pitaevskii equation to simulate finite-temperature equilibrium states in a harmonic plus quartic trap, extracting vortex configurations and analyzing correlation functions and defect statistics.
result: Identifies clear signatures of the two-step Kosterlitz–Thouless–Halperin–Nelson–Young melting scenario and shows that finite-size effects significantly affect the melting temperature at lower rotation frequencies.
conclusion: The study provides a detailed numerical characterization of vortex lattice melting phases and highlights the importance of finite-size effects, but does not directly contribute to quantum information or thermodynamics as defined in the research interests.

title: Direct Derivation Of The Modified Langevin Noise Formalism From The Canonical Quantization Of Macroscopic Electromagnetism
authors: A Ciattoni
abstract: The modified Langevin noise formalism (MLNF) models the interaction of the quantized electromagnetic field with an arbitrary lossy magneto-dielectric object placed in vacuum using three types of non-interacting bosonic polaritons: scattering, electric, and magnetic. These respectively represent free-space photons scattered by the object, and photons radiated by quantized electric and magnetic dipolar sources embedded within its volume. Recently (Ciattoni 2024 Phys. Rev. A110 013707), this formalism was justified from the canonical quantization of macroscopic electromagnetism (CQME) (Philbin 2010 New J. Phys.12 123008) in the Heisenberg picture. This was achieved by identifying the polariton operators within the formal solution of the macroscopic Maxwell equations, assuming they obey bosonic commutation relations to retrieve the canonical ones, and showing they diagonalize the CQME Hamiltonian. However, the explicit functional dependence of these polaritons on the underlying canonical field operators remained undetermined. In this paper, we derive the exact analytical expressions for the polariton operators in terms of the canonical CQME field operators. Using these mappings, we provide a direct and rigorous derivation of the MLNF from the canonical theory in the Schrödinger picture. Our derivation is structured in three foundational steps: 1) adopting the derived analytical expressions as the constitutive definitions of the polariton operators; 2) mathematically proving that these operators are strictly bosonic as a direct consequence of the canonical commutation relations; and 3) demonstrating that they exactly diagonalize the macroscopic CQME Hamiltonian.
tldr: This paper derives explicit analytical expressions for polariton operators in the modified Langevin noise formalism from canonical quantization of macroscopic electromagnetism.
motivation: The modified Langevin noise formalism (MLNF) models quantized electromagnetic field interaction with lossy media, but the explicit functional dependence of polariton operators on canonical field operators was unknown.
method: The authors derive exact analytical mappings for scattering, electric, and magnetic polariton operators in terms of canonical field operators, prove they satisfy bosonic commutation relations, and show they diagonalize the Hamiltonian.
result: The derived expressions provide a direct and rigorous derivation of MLNF from canonical quantization in the Schrödinger picture.
conclusion: The work establishes a firm theoretical foundation for MLNF, but it is a purely formal development in macroscopic electromagnetism quantization without direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: A Frequency-domain Identifiability Law For Deterministic Reconstruction Of Complex Networks Under Partial Observability
authors: Tianlong Fan And Linyuan Lü Xiaoxiao Liang
abstract: Inferring network architecture from partial behavioral observations is central to computational studies of complex systems, with implications for detecting covert actors in terrorist networks, localizing unobserved brain regions, and revealing latent molecular regulators. Focusing on evolutionary game dynamics, we uncover an empirically consistent frequency-domain regularity: the aggregated magnitude of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of a node’s payoff time series scales linearly with its structural degree, , across tested topologies and parameter regimes. Leveraging this structure–behavior scaling, we develop a deterministic inference framework that (i) estimates degrees directly from DFT spectra via a single global-slope fit, and (ii) uses brief, identifiability-oriented local interventions (‘suppress-and-measure’) to reveal adjacencies through intervention-induced spectral drops. Discrepancies between estimated degree and revealed neighbors deterministically enumerate external edges to hidden components and yield tight lower/upper bounds on the number of unobserved nodes. We analyze the conditions under which the scaling holds, quantify deviations under structural heterogeneity, and characterize sample-length dependence. Experiments on synthetic and empirical networks demonstrate accurate topology recovery, robustness to stochasticity, and scalability to thousand-node graphs, with consistent gains over causality-, correlation-, information-, and likelihood-based baselines. These results establish a DFT-based route to structure discovery under partial observability, translating local spectral measurements into actionable structural information.
tldr: This paper proposes a frequency-domain method to infer network structure from partial observations of evolutionary game dynamics.
motivation: Inferring network architecture from partial behavioral data is important for detecting covert actors, localizing brain regions, and revealing molecular regulators.
method: The authors discover a linear scaling between the DFT magnitude of node payoff time series and node degree, and develop a deterministic inference framework using spectral measurements and local interventions.
result: The method accurately recovers network topology, provides bounds on unobserved nodes, and outperforms baselines on synthetic and empirical networks.
conclusion: DFT-based spectral measurements can be translated into actionable structural information for complex networks under partial observability.

title: Strong Field Ionized Electron Trajectories Driven By Squeezed Light
authors: Alex Schimmoller And Alexandra S Landsman
abstract: In atomic strong field ionization, a photoelectron’s motion is largely determined by the laser pulse’s expected electric field, as well as the atomic potential. However, when the ionization is performed by squeezed light, the photon’s quantum statistics can modify these dynamics. In this work, we generalize the classical trajectory Monte–Carlo technique to study strong field ionization by squeezed states of light. We find that electrons driven by phase-squeezed pulses exhibit increases in longitudinal momentum consistent with what is expected from the field statistics. Meanwhile, the transverse momentum distribution shows varying influence of ‘hard’ and ‘soft’ rescattering off the Coulomb potential, and the proportion of electrons recaptured as Rydberg states decreases monotonically with the amount of squeezed light applied. This work demonstrates the added experimental control over ultrafast electron dynamics achievable by tuning light’s quantum statistics, as well as the essential role of the atomic potential in strong field ionization.
tldr: This paper studies electron trajectories in strong field ionization driven by squeezed light, focusing on the effect of quantum statistics on ultrafast electron dynamics.
motivation: To understand how squeezed light modifies electron dynamics in strong field ionization, potentially offering new control over ultrafast processes.
method: Generalizes classical trajectory Monte Carlo technique to include squeezed states of light, simulating electron trajectories under phase-squeezed pulses.
result: Phase-squeezed pulses increase longitudinal momentum as expected from field statistics; transverse momentum distribution shows varying rescattering effects; Rydberg recapture decreases with squeezing.
conclusion: Squeezed light provides additional experimental control over ultrafast electron dynamics, and the atomic potential plays an essential role in strong field ionization.

title: Vortex Solitons In Disclination Quasicrystals
authors: Hua Zhong, Yaroslav V Kartashov, Yongdong Li, Fangwei Ye And Yiqi Zhang
abstract: Quasicrystals are ubiquitous in nature. They represent unique aperiodic materials featuring long-range order that occupy an intermediate niche between exactly periodic and disordered materials. These properties are reflected in the unusual evolutionary dynamics of excitations and unique localization properties of linear eigenmodes supported by quasicrystals. In particular, being the structures characterized by discrete rotational symmetry of order , photonic quasicrystals can support the stable propagation of linear vortex-carrying light beams and vortex solitons. However, the impact of discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals on the properties of vortex light states has not been investigated so far, as only the systems constructed using the simplest Penrose tiling or corresponding optically induced Penrose lattices are considered in this context. Here, we propose a broad class of quasicrystals with global topological defects—disclinations—introduced into their structure that allows to produce novel quasicrystalline structures with any desired order of discrete rotational symmetry from the basic Penrose structure. Such global topological deformation substantially enriches the linear spectrum of quasicrystals, allowing them to support new types of linear vortex states and bifurcating from them families of stable thresholdless vortex solitons with unusual intensity and phase distributions. We find two different classes of stable vortex solitons comprising in-phase or out-of-phase pairs of closely located bright spots, with total intensity distribution reflecting a particular discrete rotational symmetry of the quasicrystal with disclination. Remarkably, even low-charge vortex solitons can be stable in quasicrystals with disclinations, whereas stability intervals for them broaden with the decrease of the discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals. Our results extend the theory of localization in quasicrystals to structures with global topological deformation, highlighting emerging prospects for the robust transmission of power or information arising in these systems.
tldr: This paper studies vortex solitons in photonic quasicrystals with disclinations, focusing on nonlinear wave propagation and localization.
motivation: To understand how global topological defects (disclinations) in quasicrystals affect the properties of vortex light states, which have not been investigated before.
method: The authors propose a class of quasicrystals with disclinations, analyze their linear spectrum, and numerically find families of stable vortex solitons.
result: Two classes of stable vortex solitons are found, with stability intervals broadening as discrete rotational symmetry decreases.
conclusion: The results extend localization theory to quasicrystals with topological deformations, offering potential for robust transmission of power or information.

title: Direct Visualization Of Field-driven Valence Band Modulation In Electrostatically Reconfigured Graphene Devices
authors: Umidakhon Rayimjonova, Chin-Yi Huang, Yi-Cheng Weng, Elin Cartwright, Fredrik O L Johansson, Noemi Vannucchi, Pavel Dudin, Avila Jose, Pei Ding, David Muradas-Belinchón, Henry Nameirakpam, Zhaojun Li, Andreas Lindblad And M Venkata Kamalakar
abstract: Graphene with ultrathin metal-oxide layers has emerged as a scalable platform for integrated electronic, spintronic, and neuromorphic devices. The in-plane electric fields in such devices are typically inferred indirectly from transport measurements, which do not provide microscopic details of the interface potential profile. Here, we use photoemission microscopy to uncover the precise electrostatic landscape of a complete device comprising diverse, heterogeneous ultrathin metal-oxide-covered graphene junctions. Using in operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution, we directly image the real potential profile across an entire graphene device, including regions covered by AlOx and TiOx nanometer-thick overlayers. Tracking the valence band edge under current bias and gate voltage enables quantitative analysis of internal field evolution via a spectroscopic screening factor, revealing an up to more than 50% suppression of the electric field in graphene covered with oxides, in agreement with transport measurements. This demonstrates local reconfiguration of electric fields in graphene for advanced two-dimensional (2D) device engineering and circuitry, while our operando circuit spectroscopy measurements provide a generic means to uncover intricate potential landscapes and carrier redistribution in 2D electronic and spintronic circuits.
tldr: This paper uses photoemission microscopy to directly visualize the electrostatic potential profile in graphene devices with oxide overlayers, revealing field suppression.
motivation: Understanding the microscopic electrostatic landscape in graphene devices is crucial for optimizing electronic and spintronic performance, but indirect transport measurements lack spatial detail.
method: The authors employ in operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution to image the valence band edge across a graphene device under bias and gate voltage, extracting a spectroscopic screening factor.
result: They observe up to 50% suppression of the electric field in graphene regions covered by AlOx and TiOx, consistent with transport measurements.
conclusion: Operando circuit spectroscopy provides a generic method to map potential landscapes in 2D devices, enabling advanced engineering of electric fields in graphene circuits.

title: Estimating The Amount Of Computation Done By A Brain Using Population Neural Activity
authors: Junang Liyuzheng Linanuj Kumar Sharmaandrew M. Leiferdavid H. Wolpertahttps://ror.org/00hx57361department Of Physics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544bhttps://ror.org/00hx57361princeton Neuroscience Institute, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08540chttps://ror.org/01arysc35santa Fe Institute, Santa Fe, NM 87501dinternational Center For Theoretical Physics, Trieste I-34151, Italyehttps://ror.org/023dz9m50complexity Science Hub, Vienna 1080, Austriafhttps://ror.org/03efmqc40arizona State University, Tempe, AZ 85287
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 25, June 2026.
SignificanceQuantifying the “amount of computation” a dynamic system performs is crucial for linking theoretical computer science to real-world processes like neural activity. We introduce a broadly applicable data-driven framework defining the “amount of ...
tldr: This paper proposes a data-driven framework to estimate the amount of computation performed by a brain using population neural activity.
motivation: Quantifying computation in dynamic systems like the brain is crucial for linking theoretical computer science to real-world processes.
method: The authors introduce a framework that analyzes population neural activity data to estimate the computational amount, likely using information-theoretic or thermodynamic measures.
result: The framework is applied to neural data, providing estimates of computation in the brain.
conclusion: The approach offers a way to bridge computation theory and neuroscience, but its relevance to quantum information or thermodynamics is indirect.

title: Vector Representation Of Exact Soliton Dynamics In Multi-component Nonlinear Schr\"odinger Systems
authors: Maxime Foucher, Laurent Delisle, Amine Jaouadi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27569v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multicomponent nonlinear Schr\"odinger equations constitute fundamental models for coherent matter waves in multicomponent Bose--Einstein condensates, spinor quantum fluids, and vector nonlinear optical systems. We develop a vector formulation of the Hirota bilinear formalism for the completely integrable Manakov system that treats the coupled nonlinear Schr\"odinger equations directly at the vector level rather than through the conventional component-wise decomposition. This framework naturally retains the intrinsic multicomponent representation of the model while providing compact analytical expressions for exact vector soliton solutions. Within this approach, we systematically construct bright, dark, and mixed one-, two-, and three-soliton solutions and show how the underlying vector structure provides a unified description of their nonlinear interactions. In particular, the proposed formalism makes the coupling between the different components explicit while preserving the geometric organization of the vector system throughout the bilinearization procedure. Beyond its analytical simplicity, the framework offers a natural perspective for the study of coherent multicomponent nonlinear excitations and provides a foundation for extending vector Hirota methods to other classes of exact solutions, including rogue waves, periodic waves, and rational solutions.
tldr: This paper develops a vector formulation of the Hirota bilinear method for the Manakov system, providing exact soliton solutions for multicomponent nonlinear Schrödinger equations.
motivation: To treat coupled nonlinear Schrödinger equations directly at the vector level, preserving the multicomponent structure and simplifying the derivation of exact soliton solutions.
method: A vector generalization of the Hirota bilinear formalism is applied to the completely integrable Manakov system, constructing bright, dark, and mixed soliton solutions up to three solitons.
result: Compact analytical expressions for vector soliton solutions are obtained, with explicit coupling between components and a unified description of nonlinear interactions.
conclusion: The vector framework offers analytical simplicity and a foundation for extending Hirota methods to other exact solutions like rogue waves and periodic waves.

title: Vibrational High-harmonics And Period-doubling Bifurcation Probed By Time-resolved Electron Diffraction
authors: Alexander Schr\"oder, Kai Nettersheim, Ferdinand Evers, Sascha Sch\"afer
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27891v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nanoscale mechanical oscillators exhibit a plethora of nonlinear phenomena with promising applications for the sensing and clocking of processes down to atomic length scales. Oscillator dynamics are typically probed by electrical or optical means, providing only limited access to the spatial profile of the oscillator motion. Here, we introduce event-based convergent beam electron diffraction for the spatio-temporal mapping of nanoscale mechanical resonators in ultrafast transmission electron microscopy. Employing an optically driven silicon membrane resonator at various driving strengths, we gain access to nonlinear processes with increasing complexity, ranging from a simple Duffing behavior to nonlinear multimode coupling and period-doubling bifurcations. The time-resolved diffraction probing approach supports a spatial resolution down to a few nanometers and a temporal resolution of 5 ns and provides quantitative information on the local membrane bending. Because the diffraction signal responds to local displacement gradients, which become more pronounced as resonators shrink, this approach offers a route toward probing nonlinear nanomechanics at the atomic scale.
tldr: This paper uses time-resolved electron diffraction to study nonlinear dynamics in nanomechanical resonators.
motivation: Understanding nonlinear phenomena in nanoscale oscillators is important for sensing and clocking applications, but existing probing methods lack spatial resolution.
method: The authors introduce event-based convergent beam electron diffraction in ultrafast transmission electron microscopy to map the spatio-temporal motion of an optically driven silicon membrane resonator.
result: They observe nonlinear processes including Duffing behavior, multimode coupling, and period-doubling bifurcations, achieving nanometer spatial and 5 ns temporal resolution.
conclusion: This diffraction-based approach provides quantitative local bending information and could enable probing nonlinear nanomechanics at atomic scales.

title: Nonextensive Statistical Signatures Of The Bilaterian Transition In Proteome Length Distributions
authors: Sertac Eroglu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protein length distributions across the tree of life carry a quantitative signature of organismal complexity. Nonextensive statistical mechanics, through the Tsallis generalized entropy formalism, provides a natural framework for describing complex systems characterized by long-range correlations, scale invariance, and hierarchical organization -- features that classical Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics cannot accommodate. In this work, the complementary cumulative distribution function (CCDF) of protein lengths is analyzed within this framework for the reference proteomes of 22 fully sequenced organisms spanning the domains Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukarya, with deliberate sampling across the animal transition zone from sponges and cnidarians to higher bilaterians. Maximum likelihood (MLE) fitting of truncated discrete q-exponential distributions, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs) reveals that the entropic index q resolves into three statistically distinct regimes: superextensive (q < 1) for prokaryotes, unicellular and non-animal multicellular eukaryotes, and basal animals; a boundary regime (CI on spanning unity) for the two cnidarians studied and the basal bilaterian C. teleta; and subextensive (q > 1) for all higher bilaterians, with q increasing monotonically across the four deuterostomes sampled from S. purpuratus (1.033) to H. sapiens (1.147). The q-exponential outperforms the ordinary exponential distribution across all 22 proteomes and becomes progressively more competitive against alternative two-parameter distributions as proteome complexity increases. These results identify the Tsallis entropic index as a continuous, physically interpretable indicator of proteome organizational complexity and extend the applicability of nonextensive statistical mechanics to proteomic systems.
tldr: This paper applies nonextensive statistical mechanics to analyze protein length distributions across species, identifying the Tsallis entropic index as a marker of organismal complexity.
motivation: To find a quantitative signature of organismal complexity in proteome length distributions that classical Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics cannot capture.
method: Fits truncated discrete q-exponential distributions to complementary cumulative distribution functions of protein lengths for 22 organisms using maximum likelihood estimation with bootstrap confidence intervals.
result: The entropic index q resolves into three regimes: superextensive (q<1) for prokaryotes and basal animals, boundary (q≈1) for cnidarians and a basal bilaterian, and subextensive (q>1) for higher bilaterians, increasing monotonically with complexity.
conclusion: The Tsallis entropic index serves as a continuous, physically interpretable indicator of proteome organizational complexity, extending nonextensive statistical mechanics to proteomic systems.

title: Fast-Mixing Markov Chains Without Gradients
authors: Robert Scheichl Robert Kutri
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most approaches for accelerating Markov chain mixing either rely on incorporating expensive geometric information in the proposals, or reduce the per-step cost of sampling via surrogate densities. We propose a localisation principle that allows a surrogate-based Metropolis-Hastings proposal to exploit gradient-level geometric information of the target density, without evaluating either the target gradient or the surrogate gradient. The construction relies on regularisation and tempering of the proposal measure. We show that the expected proposal displacement coincides with the Langevin drift up to controlled error. The resulting framework, Delayed Acceptance with Regularisation and Tempering (DART), achieves an [MATH] mixing time from warm start for strongly log-concave targets with condition number [MATH] in [MATH] dimensions. This matches the known [MATH] rate for MALA when [MATH], and scales as [MATH], independent of dimension, otherwise. This is, to our knowledge, the first mixing time guarantee for a surrogate-transition-based MCMC method. We demonstrate DART on a hierarchical spatial generalised linear mixed model. In this setting, the Dirichlet-Neumann averaging parametrisation, originally introduced for the efficient simulation of Gaussian processes, is repurposed to supply the surrogate, and its linear memory and log-linear arithmetic scaling in the number of observation sites carry over to inference.
tldr: This paper proposes a gradient-free MCMC method using surrogate densities and regularization to achieve fast mixing for strongly log-concave targets.
motivation: Accelerating Markov chain mixing typically requires expensive gradient information or surrogate densities; the authors aim to achieve fast mixing without evaluating gradients of the target or surrogate.
method: They introduce a localisation principle that allows a surrogate-based Metropolis-Hastings proposal to exploit gradient-level geometric information via regularization and tempering, without explicit gradient computation.
result: The method achieves O(κ^2 d log(κ)) mixing time from warm start for strongly log-concave targets, matching MALA when κ=O(1) and scaling as O(d log d) otherwise.
conclusion: DART provides the first mixing time guarantee for surrogate-transition-based MCMC and demonstrates practical efficiency on a hierarchical spatial GLMM.

title: Policy Gradient Learning For Distributionally Robust Markov Decision Processes Under Wasserstein Ambiguity
authors: Yadh Hafsi, Samy Mekkaoui, Huy\^en Pham, Kaixin Yan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) under distributional uncertainty in the transition kernels and develop a policy-gradient framework for Wasserstein distributionally robust control. Ambiguity is modeled by state-action dependent Wasserstein balls around nominal transition kernels, leading to a max-min control problem over randomized policies and admissible transition laws. Since the worst-case transition law depends implicitly on the policy parameters, the usual policy-gradient argument does not apply. We address this difficulty by using a Wasserstein dual reformulation of the robust Bellman recursion and analyzing its directional differentiability. This yields an explicit recursive characterization of the robust policy gradient. Building on this characterization, we propose a robust actor-critic algorithm and illustrate its behavior on discrete and continuous benchmark examples.
tldr: This paper develops a policy-gradient framework for distributionally robust Markov decision processes under Wasserstein ambiguity, focusing on robust control in operations research.
motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of optimizing policies in MDPs when transition kernels are uncertain, modeled by Wasserstein balls, which is a problem in robust optimization and control theory.
method: The authors derive a robust policy gradient using a Wasserstein dual reformulation of the robust Bellman recursion and analyze its directional differentiability, then propose a robust actor-critic algorithm.
result: They provide an explicit recursive characterization of the robust policy gradient and demonstrate the algorithm on discrete and continuous benchmark examples.
conclusion: The work contributes to distributionally robust reinforcement learning but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Performance Analysis And Optimal Design Of ORB-Type Grand Algorithms
authors: Wenyi Zhang Li Wan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Guessing Random Additive Noise Decoding (GRAND) performs decoding by sequentially guessing channel error patterns (EPs). Ordered Reliability Bits GRAND (ORBGRAND) is a notable instance suitable for efficient implementation, as it schedules EPs solely according to the ranking of soft channel outputs. In this paper, we generalize this principle to a broader class of GRAND algorithms whose testing order depends only on reliability ranking, referred to as ORB-type GRAND. We develop a unified analytical framework based on a key quantity termed the average guessing posterior (AGP), which captures the effectiveness of each EP and reduces decoding into an ordering problem over the EP space. For random code ensembles, we derive exact expressions for the block error rate (BLER), stopping-time distribution, and average number of tests under a fixed test budget. The analysis separates target-miss and target-preemption errors and shows that ordering EPs by non-increasing AGP is optimal over the EP set under consideration. For fixed linear block codes, we derive the BLER expression that isolates the code-dependent target-preemption term and characterize this term through higher-order weight relationships of codeword tuples, with a computable first-order upper bound as a useful special case. Guided by these insights, we formulate ReShuffled-ORBGRAND (RS-ORBGRAND) as an offline AGP-based reshuffling scheme. Numerical results for the Bose--Chaudhuri--Hocquenghem (BCH)[MATH] code show that RS-ORBGRAND consistently improves existing ORB-type GRAND algorithms and lies within [MATH]~dB of a maximum-likelihood decoding lower-bound benchmark at a BLER of [MATH].
tldr: This paper analyzes and optimizes ORB-type GRAND decoding algorithms for classical error correction, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To improve the performance of ORBGRAND decoding by developing a unified analytical framework and an optimal ordering scheme.
method: Introduces the average guessing posterior (AGP) metric to capture EP effectiveness, derives exact BLER expressions for random code ensembles and fixed linear block codes, and proposes RS-ORBGRAND.
result: RS-ORBGRAND outperforms existing ORB-type algorithms and approaches maximum-likelihood decoding within 0.1 dB for BCH codes.
conclusion: The AGP-based ordering is optimal and the reshuffling scheme yields practical gains, but the work is purely classical coding theory.

title: Analysis Of Nonlinear Random Polarization In Dispersive Dielectrics
authors: Emmanuel E. Oguadimma Nathan L. Gibson
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27445v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a study on the time-domain propagation of electromagnetic waves in dielectric materials modeled by a nonlinear Debye medium with random perturbations. Polynomial Chaos Expansions are employed to transform the random nonlinear Debye polarization model into a deterministic framework. We extend the Yee discretization to the resulting coupled system, establish second order accuracy, and verify convergence numerically. We investigate the sensitivity of nonlinear properties to uncertainty, particularly when the amplitude of the input signal is large. Given the challenges in manufacturing where uncertainties can cause optimal parameters to vary and potentially disrupt nonlinear effects, our approach incorporates these uncertainties within the simulation. This can enable the model-based design identification of realizable materials that maintain their desired effects despite variations. The findings from this study contribute to a deeper understanding of wave propagation in complex media, with potential implications for applications in optical communications, material science, and electromagnetic wave control.
tldr: This paper studies nonlinear random polarization in dispersive dielectrics using polynomial chaos expansions and numerical simulations.
motivation: To understand wave propagation in complex media with uncertainties, which is relevant for optical communications and material science.
method: Polynomial Chaos Expansions transform the random nonlinear Debye polarization model into a deterministic framework; Yee discretization is extended to the coupled system.
result: Second-order accuracy is established and convergence is verified numerically; sensitivity of nonlinear properties to uncertainty is investigated.
conclusion: The approach enables model-based design of materials that maintain desired nonlinear effects despite manufacturing variations.

title: Characterisation Of Reactive Nash Equilibria In Repeated Additive Games
authors: Franziska Lesigang, Christian Hilbe, Nikoleta E. Glynatsi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study reactive strategies in repeated additive games between two players with finitely many actions. Reactive strategies condition only on the opponent's previous action, making them one of the simplest ways players can respond to past interactions. Additive games include important models of cooperation, such as the donation game and games with a punishment option. We show that, for this class of games and strategies, the conditions for symmetric Nash equilibria reduce to a system of linear equalities and inequalities in the strategy parameters, allowing us to characterise all such equilibria. We establish a one-to-one correspondence between non-empty subsets S of the action set and equilibrium classes, which we call S-supporting equilibria. These are equilibria that use exactly the actions in S when playing against themselves. As a special case, we recover the well-known equalizer strategies as the equilibria supported on the entire action set. To assess which equilibrium classes are most evolutionarily relevant, we complement our analytical characterisation with simulations of social learning dynamics. We find that their prevalence is determined by two factors: how likely they are to be generated and how robust they are against invasion.
tldr: This paper characterizes reactive Nash equilibria in repeated additive games, focusing on cooperation models like the donation game.
motivation: Understanding reactive strategies in repeated games is important for studying cooperation, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors derive conditions for symmetric Nash equilibria as linear equalities and inequalities, and complement with simulations of social learning dynamics.
result: They establish a one-to-one correspondence between subsets of actions and equilibrium classes, recovering equalizer strategies as a special case.
conclusion: The prevalence of equilibrium classes depends on generation likelihood and robustness against invasion.

title: Observers, Symmetries, And The Hierarchy Of Language Classes: A Theory Of Computation Parameterized By The Observer
authors: Fabio F. G. Buono
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27407v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce the , a new axis of classification for formal languages, orthogonal to the Chomsky hierarchy. An observer is a function [MATH] that determines which information about the input is accessible to a computational system. The order-blind automaton, which perceives the input as a multiset of symbols rather than a sequence, constitutes the paradigmatic case. We prove that the class of languages recognisable by any machine equipped with such an observer coincides exactly with the permutation-closed languages. We then define a partial order on observers that induces a hierarchy of language classes parametrised not by the computational power of the machine, but by the structure of the observer. We prove that this hierarchy has the structure of a partial order with a diamond-shaped profile sub-lattice, comprising the length branch [MATH] and the parity branch [MATH], with [MATH] and [MATH] incomparable, and an infinite subsequence branch [MATH], both converging to the complete observer. We prove that the observational hierarchy is strictly incomparable with the Chomsky hierarchy, and introduce the notion of of a language. We further define observer-parametrised complexity classes [MATH] and [MATH], and show that computational hardness and structural blindness are two independent phenomena. In particular, [MATH] holds as a structural collapse strictly inside [MATH].
tldr: This paper introduces a new classification axis for formal languages based on observers, which is orthogonal to the Chomsky hierarchy, and explores its implications for computational complexity.
motivation: The authors aim to generalize formal language theory by parameterizing computational systems by the information accessible to them, rather than by their computational power alone.
method: They define observers as functions that determine which aspects of the input are visible, and study the resulting language classes and complexity classes.
result: They prove that the observer hierarchy is strictly incomparable with the Chomsky hierarchy and that computational hardness and structural blindness are independent.
conclusion: The work provides a new perspective on language classification and complexity, but is purely theoretical and unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Co-Optimization Of Analog Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks For Low-Power Function Approximation In Flexible Electronics
authors: Paula Carolina Lozano Duarte, Georgios Zervakis, Mehdi Tahoori, Sani Nassif
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27892v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wearable devices and Internet of Things (IoT) sensors require on-sensor processing of biosignals and environmental data, including computationally demanding operations such as nonlinear activation functions for neural network inference, sensor calibration curves to map raw readings to physical units, and signal preprocessing functions like logarithmic compression and power operations for feature extraction. These functions exhibit significant complexity, often involving transcendental operations and multivariate dependencies that are costly to implement digitally. Analog function approximation provides a power-efficient alternative by performing these computations in the analog domain, thereby reducing the energy overhead associated with analog-to-digital conversion and subsequent digital processing. Flexible Electronics (FE) present a particularly attractive platform for wearable applications due to mechanical flexibility and low-cost fabrication, but impose strict constraints on circuit density and power consumption, making efficient analog implementations critical but challenging. This work introduces Analog Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (AKANs), developed via hardware-software co-optimization, to approximate these complex multivariate functions accurately under hardware imperfections. Our method incorporates circuit-level error modeling during training and applies pruning at both software and hardware levels to reduce area and power. Validation across multiple benchmarks demonstrates that our proposed pruning methodology not only reduces hardware cost but can also improve approximation accuracy by regularizing spline parameters. Results show up to 55% area and 50% power savings, with average reductions of nearly 30% across datasets, highlighting AKANs as a robust and generalizable framework for low-power analog function approximation in FE.
tldr: This paper proposes a co-optimized analog Kolmogorov-Arnold network for low-power function approximation in flexible electronics.
motivation: Wearable and IoT devices require energy-efficient on-sensor processing of complex nonlinear functions, but digital implementations are costly. Flexible electronics impose strict area and power constraints, motivating analog approximation.
method: The authors introduce Analog Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (AKANs) with hardware-software co-optimization, incorporating circuit-level error modeling during training and applying pruning at both software and hardware levels.
result: The method achieves up to 55% area and 50% power savings with average reductions of nearly 30% across benchmarks, and pruning can improve approximation accuracy by regularizing spline parameters.
conclusion: AKANs provide a robust and generalizable framework for low-power analog function approximation in flexible electronics, suitable for wearable and IoT applications.

title: Ferromagnetism Versus Antiferromagnetism In Narrow-Band Systems: Competition Between Quantum Geometry And Band Dispersion
authors: Haoyu Hu, Oskar Vafek, Kristjan Haule, And B. Andrei Bernevig

Magnetism in narrow-band systems arises from the interplay between electronic correlations, quantum geometry, and band dispersion. In particular, both ferro and antiferro magnets are known to occur as ground states of (different) models featuring narrow bands. This poses the question of which is fav…
