We show that on an invariant open state-space domain, one iteration of Bregman ADMM defines a smooth primal--dual fixed-point map whose strict-saddle KKT points are unstable fixed points; consequently, from random initialization the iterates converge to a strict saddle with probability zero. Combined with existing first-order convergence results, this yields almost-sure second-order stationarity of limiting KKT points. We extend the analysis to a multi-block star consensus formulation for distributed optimization. The technical novelty lies in a determinant reduction with a Bregman-specific symmetrization and scaling step in the two block spectral argument, together with a null space cancellation exploiting the star graph structure in the consensus case. Numerical experiments on distributed matrix factorization illustrate the theory, and a symmetric tensor factorization example demonstrates the broader Bregman proximal splitting idea beyond the separable consensus setting.
tldr: This paper analyzes second-order KKT guarantees for Bregman ADMM in nonconvex and non-Lipschitz optimization, focusing on convergence to strict saddles.
motivation: Standard Lipschitz gradient assumptions fail for polynomial objectives in matrix and tensor models; the paper aims to provide convergence guarantees under weaker conditions.
method: The authors use a determinant reduction with Bregman-specific symmetrization and scaling in a two-block spectral argument, plus null space cancellation for star graph consensus.
result: They show that from random initialization, iterates converge to a strict saddle with probability zero, ensuring almost-sure second-order stationarity of limiting KKT points.
conclusion: The work extends first-order convergence results to second-order stationarity for a class of nonconvex problems, with applications in distributed optimization.

title: Two-Dimensional Locally Adaptive Non-Hydrostatic Extension Of Shallow Water Equations
authors: J\"orn Behrens Kemal Firdaus
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27562v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce a two-dimensional non-hydrostatic model for shallow water wave dispersion. The model is based on a locally adapted application of a non-hydrostatic correction to the hydrostatic shallow water equations (SWE) in a predictor-corrector scheme. Applying the non-hydrostatic correction uniformly to the entire domain demands a high computational cost, since an elliptic system of equations needs to be solved for the correction terms. We demonstrate that by determining the area where the non-hydrostatic effects are significant, and applying the correction only locally, the computational effort can be reduced by approximately 40\% without sacrificing accuracy in tsunami-like scenarios. As indicators for the non-hydrostatic effect, we use the ratio between total water depth and surface elevation, as well as horizontal velocity norms. Results are shown for several well-known test cases, including wave trains over a semi-circular shoal, static, and moving bottom tsunami-like wave propagation.
tldr: This paper presents a computational method to efficiently simulate non-hydrostatic effects in shallow water equations for tsunami-like scenarios.
motivation: Uniform non-hydrostatic correction is computationally expensive; the authors aim to reduce cost by applying correction only where needed.
method: They use local indicators (water depth to surface elevation ratio, horizontal velocity norms) to identify regions requiring non-hydrostatic correction, then apply a predictor-corrector scheme locally.
result: The local approach reduces computational effort by about 40% without significant loss of accuracy in tsunami-like test cases.
conclusion: Locally adaptive non-hydrostatic correction is a viable method to improve efficiency of shallow water simulations for tsunami propagation.

title: Auditing Ai Investment Recommendations As Executable Actions
authors: Sidnei Barbieri, Wellington Vargas, \'agney Lopes Roth Ferraz
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27570v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI systems increasingly produce investment recommendations, yet the usual evaluations ask the wrong question. Realized return is noisy and easy to overfit, and agreement with a reference portfolio can reward advice that cannot be executed. We argue that an AI-generated recommendation should first be audited as an executable financial action, and only then judged on return. We make this concrete with a deterministic, replayable baseline and a protocol that scores any advisor on three properties a single number conflates: validity under portfolio and fee constraints, stability across repeated runs, and agreement with the baseline. These properties separate cleanly, and agreement is the most misleading in isolation: across a 120-scenario bank, the control that agrees most with the baseline (0.94) is admissible in only 0.58 of its runs, so agreement certifies an invalid action in 42% of them. On an adversarial set, two frontier models are admissible in barely half of their bare-prompt runs and fail on order arithmetic, not judgment; supplying the fee arithmetic deterministically lifts both to near-perfect validity. We make no alpha claim: the baseline is a transparent verifier whose guardrails follow from the fee schedule and whose decisions replay from frozen inputs, and every figure and table regenerates offline from the artifact.
tldr: This paper proposes a framework for auditing AI-generated investment recommendations by evaluating their executability under portfolio and fee constraints, rather than relying solely on return or agreement metrics.
motivation: Standard evaluations of AI investment advice focus on realized return or agreement with a reference portfolio, which can be noisy, overfitted, or reward advice that cannot actually be executed.
method: The authors introduce a deterministic, replayable baseline and a protocol that scores an advisor on three separate properties: validity under portfolio and fee constraints, stability across repeated runs, and agreement with the baseline.
result: Across a 120-scenario bank, the control that agrees most with the baseline is admissible in only 58% of runs, showing that agreement alone certifies invalid actions 42% of the time. Frontier models fail on order arithmetic, but providing fee arithmetic deterministically lifts validity to near-perfect.
conclusion: AI-generated investment recommendations should first be audited for executability before judging their return, and the proposed framework provides a transparent, replayable method for such auditing.

title: AdvScan: Black-Box Adversarial Example Detection At Runtime Through Power Analysis
authors: Michael Zuzak Robi Paul
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27704v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: TinyML models deployed on edge devices are increasingly adopted in safety/security-critical applications, making them a prime target for adversarial example (AE) attacks where inputs are modified to cause misclassifications. However, existing AE detection methods either require white-box model access, which is often unavailable in licensed black-box deployments, or rely on input pre-processing stages that add non-trivial latency and resource overhead, often exceeding what mission-critical applications can afford on their inference path. To address these challenges, we propose AdvScan, a runtime power analysis-based methodology for AE detection that operates in a black-box scenario while inducing minimal latency. AdvScan is based on the observation that AEs produce anomalous neuron activations, which in turn generate distinctive power-consumption signatures. The algorithm initially constructs a baseline distribution of power signatures from known benign inputs; then, at runtime, it applies a one-sample t-test to determine whether a test input's power signature significantly deviates from this baseline, thereby detecting AEs. We evaluated AdvScan using three adversarial example generation algorithms: Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM), Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), and Carlini-Wagner (C&W), on three MLPerf Tiny benchmark models implemented on two target devices: the STM32F303RC (ARM Cortex-M4) and STM32L562RE (ARM Cortex-M33) microcontrollers. Across 318,400 total test inputs, AdvScan detects 99.984% of AEs with only 40 false negatives and zero false positives. These results demonstrate the viability of power-based AE detection for secure, accuracy-critical TinyML deployments in black-box environments.
tldr: This paper proposes a black-box adversarial example detection method for TinyML devices using power analysis.
motivation: Existing adversarial example detection methods require white-box model access or add latency, which is unsuitable for black-box TinyML deployments in safety-critical applications.
method: AdvScan builds a baseline power signature distribution from benign inputs and uses a one-sample t-test at runtime to detect deviations caused by adversarial examples.
result: On 318,400 test inputs across two microcontrollers and three attack algorithms, AdvScan detects 99.984% of adversarial examples with zero false positives.
conclusion: Power-based adversarial example detection is viable for secure TinyML deployments in black-box environments with minimal latency.

title: Exploring And Exploiting Synchrony Limitations Of Time-Triggered Network-Agnostic Guardians
authors: Shreya Vithal Kulhalli, Mohammad Ibrahim Alkoudsi, Gerhard Fohler
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27819v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-triggered communication protocols rely on trusted components known as guardians to enforce adherence to predetermined network schedules. Network-agnostic guardians offer an efficient and scalable distributed solution with reduced implementation cost and complexity compared to network-aware alternatives. However, this efficiency is based on the guardian's dependence on the controlled node for clock synchronization, which introduces a vulnerability: a malicious node can exploit this dependency to launch timing attacks against its guardian and eventually interfere with messages from other nodes on the network. In this paper, we establish a theoretical lower bound on the attainable clock synchronization precision between a node and its network-agnostic guardian. Building on this result, we introduce a timing attack that leverages the unavoidably imperfect clock synchrony to cause controlled and undetected de-synchronization of the guardian. The attack enables a malicious node to cause collisions with targeted critical network messages. We evaluate the effectiveness of the attack using a FlexRay field bus network model implemented in the OMNeT++ simulation framework. Our results show that the attack is able to remain undetected with 100% success and disrupts the transmission of the critical messages of the target node by causing collisions with them with 100% success.
tldr: This paper studies clock synchronization vulnerabilities in time-triggered network guardians, with no connection to quantum information theory.
motivation: Network-agnostic guardians rely on node clock synchronization, which can be exploited by malicious nodes to launch timing attacks.
method: The authors derive a theoretical lower bound on clock synchronization precision and design a timing attack that causes undetected de-synchronization, evaluated via FlexRay bus simulation in OMNeT++.
result: The attack achieves 100% undetected success and 100% collision rate with critical messages.
conclusion: The work highlights a fundamental vulnerability in network-agnostic guardians due to unavoidable clock synchrony imperfections.

title: Parameterized Verification Of Asynchronous Round-Based Distributed Algorithms Via Reduction To Finite-Counter Systems
authors: Nathalie Bertrand, Pranav Ghorpade, Sasha Rubin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional model-checking techniques typically verify distributed algorithms only for a fixed number of finite-state processes. Parameterized model checking generalizes this to any number of processes, while still typically assuming that each process is finite-state. In this work, we consider asynchronous round-based distributed algorithms in which each process is infinite-state since it can execute for an infinite number of rounds. We show that the parameterized verification problem for asynchronous round-based distributed algorithms is undecidable, already for simple specifications. Nevertheless, as our main contribution, we provide a reduction to LTL model checking over finite-counter systems and prove that it is sound and complete. This enables the use of off-the-shelf, mature symbolic model checkers for finite-counter systems. We demonstrate the practical applicability of this reduction by verifying safety and liveness properties of several asynchronous round-based consensus and leader-election algorithms using the nuXmv model checker.
tldr: This paper addresses parameterized verification of asynchronous round-based distributed algorithms, which is unrelated to quantum information theory.
motivation: Parameterized verification of distributed algorithms is important but the paper focuses on classical distributed computing, not quantum systems.
method: The authors show undecidability of the parameterized verification problem and provide a reduction to LTL model checking over finite-counter systems.
result: The reduction is sound and complete, enabling verification of safety and liveness properties using existing model checkers.
conclusion: The work contributes to classical distributed algorithm verification, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Combining Axiomatic Models For Refinement Proofs
authors: Alperen Dogan Suha Orhun Mutluergil
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Refinement proofs verify an implementation by showing that its behaviours are subsumed by a simpler specification, on which safety properties are easier to establish. We study how such proofs interact with the axiomatic program logics used to verify the specification. We first give a uniform account of Hoare, Incorrectness, Lisbon, and Necessary-Preconditions logic, classified by the direction in which each constrains a transition and by whether it over- or under-approximates its target set. We then show that simulation relations transfer state-based safety properties: a forward simulation carries a Hoare (inductive) invariant of the specification to one of the implementations, and forward and backward simulations both carry ordinary invariants, via the pre-image of the relation. Finally, we characterize, within these logics, when a relation is a simulation, forward simulations by the validity of Hoare or Lisbon triples, backward simulations by Necessary-Preconditions or Incorrectness triples, so that the simulation obligation reduces to a triple in an off-the-shelf functional logic. We illustrate the development with a concurrent counter, transporting a safety bound from an atomic sequential specification to a Left--Right implementation through an intermediate nondeterministic-concurrent counter, with a forward simulation on one side and a backward simulation on the other.
tldr: This paper studies refinement proofs in the context of axiomatic program logics, focusing on simulation relations and safety property transfer.
motivation: To understand how refinement proofs interact with axiomatic program logics and to characterize simulation relations within these logics.
method: The authors provide a uniform account of Hoare, Incorrectness, Lisbon, and Necessary-Preconditions logic, and show how forward and backward simulations transfer safety properties.
result: They characterize forward simulations by validity of Hoare or Lisbon triples, and backward simulations by Necessary-Preconditions or Incorrectness triples.
conclusion: The work reduces simulation obligations to triples in off-the-shelf functional logic, illustrated with a concurrent counter example.

title: Provable Reductions In Tfnp
authors: Noah Fleming, Stefan Grosser, Toniann Pitassi, Robert Robere
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a new family of propositional proof systems, denoted , for an arbitrary TFNP search problem [MATH]. Informally, a refutation of a CNF formula [MATH] in is given by a polynomial-time reduction from the false-clause search problem [MATH] to [MATH], combined with an Extended Frege proof that the reduction is correct. These are motivated in two ways: 1. They are the propositional translations of witnessing theorems in bounded arithmetic, by which proofs of [MATH] formulas [MATH] in a theory [MATH] imply algorithms solving the search problem for [MATH] in a TFNP class corresponding to [MATH]. 2. They are a white-box analogue of the characterizations of proof systems using decision tree reductions to black-box TFNP problems. We consider the proof system , where Iter is a complete problem for PLS. We prove that is polynomially equivalent to the sequent calculus [MATH], and also to the implicit Resolution proof system [EF, Resolution]. Hence [MATH] and [EF, Resolution] are equivalent, which is the first characterization of an implicit proof system by a classical proof system beyond the work of Wang. We also consider for general TFNP relations [MATH]. We observe that if EF can prove that a search problem [MATH] is in FP, then is polynomially equivalent to EF. This contrasts to our above result, which shows that Extended-Frege provable reductions to [MATH], a problem widely believed not to be in FP, yields a proof system ([MATH]) that is believed to be stronger than Extended Frege. Finally, we show that for any proof system [MATH] which is sufficiently strong, there is a polynomial-time computable search problem [MATH] FP such that is polynomially equivalent to [MATH]. Letting [MATH] [EF, Resolution] and combining our two results shows that is polynomially equivalent to .
tldr: This paper introduces a new family of propositional proof systems based on TFNP search problems and studies their equivalence to classical proof systems.
motivation: To connect TFNP search problems with propositional proof complexity and to characterize implicit proof systems via classical ones.
method: Defines proof systems parameterized by TFNP problems, shows polynomial equivalence between certain systems and existing proof systems like EF and Resolution.
result: Proves that the proof system based on the PLS-complete problem Iter is equivalent to the sequent calculus LK and to implicit Resolution; also shows that for any sufficiently strong proof system there is a TFNP problem such that the corresponding system is equivalent.
conclusion: The work provides new connections between TFNP and proof complexity, but is purely in computational complexity theory with no quantum information or thermodynamics content.

title: Agentic AI-Powered Re-Identification: An Emerging, Scalable Threat To Mobility Microdata Privacy
authors: Oscar Thees, Roman M\"uller, Matthias Templ
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The widespread collection of fine-grained location data by commercial data brokers creates a re-identification risk that is not widely recognised by the public. While prior research has established that mobility traces are highly unique and that individuals can, in principle, be identified from a handful of spatio-temporal points, such attacks have historically required significant manual effort from skilled analysts, limiting their practical scale. In this feasibility study, we demonstrate in a real world setting that agentic AI fundamentally changes this threat model. We present an end-to-end pipeline in which large language model agents autonomously search the open web, cross-reference public records and social media, and resolve raw coordinate sequences to candidate identities - without human intervention. We evaluate the pipeline on a spatio-temporal dataset containing simulated location points anchored at and around true home and work addresses, focusing on a high-risk disclosure scenario. Our results demonstrate that, from spatio-temporal data and public sources alone, our agentic AI successfully re-identified 18 of the 25 re-identifiable individuals (72%) and 18 of 43 cases overall (41.9%). We discuss implications for Statistical Disclosure Control (SDC) practice and outline the near-future escalation that data custodians and regulators must anticipate. De facto anonymity - an implicit foundation of SDC practice - is shifting. Agentic AI strengthens the case that re-identification is reasonably likely by any means under the GDPR Recital-26 standard, at costs of minutes-and-dollars per target.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that agentic AI can autonomously re-identify individuals from mobility data, posing a new threat to privacy.
motivation: Mobility traces are highly unique, but re-identification attacks previously required manual effort; this study explores whether agentic AI can automate the process at scale.
method: An end-to-end pipeline using large language model agents to search the web, cross-reference public records and social media, and resolve coordinate sequences to identities, tested on simulated location data.
result: The pipeline re-identified 72% of re-identifiable individuals (18/25) and 41.9% of all cases (18/43) from spatio-temporal data and public sources alone.
conclusion: Agentic AI makes re-identification cheap and scalable, challenging de facto anonymity and requiring updates to statistical disclosure control practices.

title: Decoys Cannot Go Everywhere: Mapping The Deception Surface In Mitre Att&ck
authors: Veronica Valeros, Carlos Catania, Viliam Lis\'y, Harm Griffioen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cyber deception research often assumes that a decoy can be placed wherever there is attacker behavior. This work tests that assumption across MITRE ATT&CK v18.1. We introduce a four-criterion rubric for infrastructure deception and apply it to all 250 ATT&CK techniques. The rubric evaluates whether a defender-controlled decoy can be placed, whether an attacker is likely to interact with it, what intelligence that interaction can yield, and whether the interaction reliably indicates malice. The resulting deception surface is sparse: only 80 techniques (32%) admit a decoy the attacker could plausibly reach. For the remaining 170 techniques, there is no defender-controlled asset in the attacker's path that can be fabricated as a decoy. Decoy placement across those 80 techniques falls into two patterns we call Sweep and Seek. In Sweep, the attacker moves broadly through assets in range and encounters the decoy as part of that activity. In Seek, the attacker looks for a specific kind of asset and interacts with a fabricated version of it. These patterns give a simple placement rule: a decoy must either sit on a sweep path or imitate a sought asset. We also show that decoys usually have useful intelligence potential, but whether an attacker interacts with them at all, and whether that interaction reliably indicates malice, both vary. We release the rubric, decision rules, and per-technique assessment as an auditable baseline for future deception research and deployment planning, and show that infrastructure decoys cannot be assumed to apply to all attacker behavior.
tldr: This paper analyzes the feasibility of cyber deception techniques across MITRE ATT&CK, finding that only 32% of techniques admit a decoy.
motivation: Cyber deception research often assumes decoys can be placed wherever attacker behavior occurs, but this assumption has not been systematically tested.
method: The authors introduce a four-criterion rubric for infrastructure deception and apply it to all 250 ATT&CK techniques to evaluate decoy placement, attacker interaction, intelligence yield, and malice indication.
result: Only 80 out of 250 techniques (32%) admit a decoy that an attacker could plausibly reach; decoy placement follows two patterns: Sweep and Seek.
conclusion: Infrastructure decoys cannot be assumed to apply to all attacker behavior, and the deception surface is sparse; the rubric and assessments provide an auditable baseline for future research.

title: Shard: Cell-keyed Residual Splitting For Alignment-resistant Private Dense Retrieval
authors: Sergey Kurilenko
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27976v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dense embeddings underpin semantic search and RAG, yet a leaked vector store hands much of the underlying text back to whoever holds it. The attacks that make this possible (few-shot alignment, zero-shot inversion, unsupervised cross-space translation) share one weakness: the protected store is a single global geometry that can be aligned to a known one. A secret global rotation, the usual lightweight defence, is no exception: orthogonal Procrustes recovers it once the attacker has about the subspace dimension in known pairs. We introduce Shard, a retrieval-preserving embedding transform that removes this weak axis. The centred embedding is split into a short public prefix (for stage-1 retrieval) and a private residual sharded into C cells under separate secret keys; the residual is reranked under CKKS, where the keys cancel and leave the inner product exact. A single parameter C runs the design from the global-linear baseline it replaces (C=1) to per-document micro-keys (C=N). Because the rerank is full-dimensional, Shard returns the raw-space nDCG@10 that half-SVD truncation gives up; and because the residual is keyed cell-locally, mapping it back to a common frame under a diffuse known-plaintext leak costs roughly C times more anchors (median 200 to 102,400 at C=256), for a few encrypted queries. The short public prefix leaks far less neighbour structure, and a micro-key limit drives the residual graph to zero with an unlinkable, renewable template. The barrier holds against learned, non-linear and unsupervised aligners, and where a matched-utility noise defence de-anonymises almost every probe, Shard de-anonymises none. We are plain about the limits: within a cell the keys cancel, a targeted attacker needs only about d_priv anchors, and an overlapping reference corpus still leaks through the prefix. Shard is an attack-aware geometric defence, not a cryptographic guarantee.
tldr: Shard is a defense against embedding inversion attacks that splits embeddings into a public prefix and private residual shards keyed per cell.
motivation: Dense embeddings used in semantic search and RAG are vulnerable to inversion attacks that reconstruct text from leaked vector stores; existing defenses like global rotations are easily broken by Procrustes alignment.
method: Shard splits each embedding into a short public prefix for retrieval and a private residual that is divided into C cells, each encrypted with a separate secret key; reranking uses CKKS homomorphic encryption where keys cancel to yield exact inner products.
result: Shard preserves full-dimensional retrieval quality (nDCG@10) while requiring roughly C times more known-plaintext anchors to break, and de-anonymizes no probes under matched-utility noise defense.
conclusion: Shard provides an attack-aware geometric defense that raises the bar for alignment attacks but is not a cryptographic guarantee; it is suitable for applications where retrieval accuracy must be maintained.

title: AdvancedShelLM: A Stateful Multi-Agent Llm Honeypot For Ssh Deception
authors: Muris Sladi\'c, Eman Alibali\'c, Veronica Valeros, Carlos Catania, Sebastian Garcia
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27990v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based SSH honeypots can generate believable interactions, but evaluations indicate they remain somewhat identifiable to determined attackers, indicating the need for a better scaffolding. We present a new LLM-based honeypot design that uses a multi-agent, multi-LLM architecture to address the limitations of the previous shelLM LLM honeypot. Our honeypot, called AdvancedShelLM, uses two LLM agents, a Manager and a Worker, that better understand the commands while reducing incorrect responses and increasing deception. It implements an advanced permanent filesystem, allowing many simultaneous attackers to see the same changing files for the first time. It was evaluated with: (i) unit tests for generative capabilities, (ii) an AI attacker (ARACNE) to assess realism and deception, (iii) human attackers to assess its deceptive capability, and (iv) an Internet deployment to evaluate deception in real-world attacks. In unit test results, AdvancedShelLM achieved a pass rate of up to 99.02%. The AI attacker ARACNE had issues making a decision if the system is honeypot or not, but showed slight bias towards saying honeypot, even for a real Ubuntu shell. With human attackers, AdvancedShelLM deceived more humans than Cowrie, but had similar results as shelLM. The Internet deployment showed concrete evidence that the output of AdvancedShelLM can influence the behaviour of real-life attackers.
tldr: This paper presents a multi-agent LLM-based honeypot for SSH deception, which is unrelated to quantum information theory.
motivation: Existing LLM-based honeypots are identifiable by determined attackers; the authors aim to improve deception through a multi-agent architecture.
method: The system uses two LLM agents (Manager and Worker) with a persistent filesystem, and is evaluated via unit tests, AI attackers, human attackers, and real-world deployment.
result: AdvancedShelLM achieved a 99.02% pass rate in unit tests, deceived more humans than Cowrie, and influenced real attacker behavior.
conclusion: The multi-agent design enhances deception and realism, but the paper is entirely outside the scope of quantum information theory.

title: Ghost Without Shell: Measuring Non-Interactive Ssh Attacks On Honeypots
authors: Veronica Valeros, Muris Sladi\'c, Sebastian Garcia
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cyber deception research has focused on improving honeypot deception capabilities to increase attacker engagement and extend their interactions to collect more and better intelligence. For SSH honeypots, this relies on the assumption that attackers log in, open a shell, and type. We tested whether this still held by deploying eleven SSH honeypots that served both interactive and non-interactive session requests for fifteen days. We collected 177,622 authenticated sessions and validated our results against an independent Cowrie dataset over the same time window. We found that 99.23% of sessions were non-interactive. Interactive sessions account for only 0.10%. The same pattern held in the comparative third-party dataset used for evaluation. This finding is important because a honeypot that focuses on interactive shells or evaluates success based on session length and the number of commands can miss most authenticated attacks and draw the wrong conclusions about what attackers do after login.
tldr: This paper studies non-interactive SSH attacks on honeypots, finding that 99.23% of authenticated sessions are non-interactive, challenging assumptions about attacker behavior.
motivation: Cyber deception research assumes attackers open a shell and type commands, but this may no longer hold. The authors test this assumption to improve honeypot design.
method: Deployed eleven SSH honeypots serving both interactive and non-interactive sessions for 15 days, collected 177,622 authenticated sessions, and validated results against an independent Cowrie dataset.
result: 99.23% of sessions were non-interactive; interactive sessions accounted for only 0.10%. The pattern was consistent in the third-party dataset.
conclusion: Honeypots focusing on interactive shells or using session length/command count as success metrics miss most authenticated attacks and draw incorrect conclusions.

title: ToolPrivacyBench: Benchmarking Purpose-Bound Privacy In Tool-Using Llm Agents
authors: Shijing Hu, Liang Liu, Zhu Meng, Zhicheng Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28061v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have increasingly moved from standalone text generation systems to agents that invoke external tools, access environments, and execute multi-step tasks. However, conventional function-calling benchmarks mainly evaluate task completion and API correctness, while privacy evaluation benchmarks typically focus on final responses or privacy judgments. Neither perspective captures purpose-bound information flow across an executed multi-tool trajectory. Motivated by this limitation in current agent evaluation, ToolPrivacyBench audits whether task-private atoms are routed only to authorized tools and downstream sinks, thereby evaluating both task completion and privacy over-disclosure during tool use. The benchmark contains 2,150 cases, including 1,150 fully synthetic privacy-sensitive business workflows and 1,000 cases adapted from existing multi-tool and function-calling benchmarks. Each case is represented by a policy knowledge base. After an agent executes against mock business backends, the evaluator compares recorded tool arguments and backend audit logs with this policy knowledge base. The evaluation covers nine widely used agents to characterize purpose-bound privacy over-disclosure. The results show that successful tool execution does not imply appropriate privacy disclosure: an agent may complete a task while transmitting unnecessary private information through intermediate tool calls. ToolPrivacyBench therefore formalizes a need-to-know disclosure boundary, under which each tool should receive only the information necessary for its stated purpose, and uses trajectory-level auditing to identify privacy over-disclosure in multi-tool workflows.
tldr: This paper introduces a benchmark for evaluating privacy over-disclosure in tool-using LLM agents, focusing on purpose-bound information flow.
motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate task completion or privacy in final responses, but fail to capture privacy leaks during multi-tool trajectories.
method: The benchmark includes 2,150 cases with policy knowledge bases; agents execute tasks against mock backends, and evaluators compare tool arguments and audit logs to the policy.
result: Experiments with nine agents show that successful task completion does not guarantee appropriate privacy disclosure; agents often transmit unnecessary private information.
conclusion: The benchmark formalizes a need-to-know disclosure boundary and uses trajectory-level auditing to identify privacy over-disclosure in multi-tool workflows.

title: GTI-mSEMP Framework : A Proposed Framework To Stimulate Malware Propagation With Inclusion Of Attacker-Defender Strategy
authors: Kristopher Wilson Shadeeb Hossain
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28079v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid proliferation of automated, multi-vector malware threats poses a significant risk to heterogeneous, resource constrained cyber-physical networks. Conventional epidemiological models often treat security defenses as static parameters, failing to capture the strategic, asymmetric maneuvers between an attacker and a defender. To address the gap, this paper proposes a Game-Theory-Integrated Modified Multi- Wireless Sensor Epidemic Malware Propagation (GTI-mSEMP) framework. This paper analyzed and compared the operational trajectories of Susceptible (S) and Recovered (R) node populations across three different operational regimes: Balanced Matchup, Exploit Surge and Hardened Defense. Numerical simulation results capture the real-time transient dynamics of the network state variables, demonstrating how the epidemic curve shifts when either the defensive or offensive scaling vectors hold an efficiency advantage. The proposed mathematical and numerical framework provides a rigorous foundation that can be deployed in highly adversarial network environments to evaluate dynamic malware propagation and predict localized node population states.
tldr: This paper proposes a game-theoretic framework for modeling malware propagation in cyber-physical networks, focusing on attacker-defender strategies.
motivation: Conventional epidemiological models treat security defenses as static, failing to capture strategic interactions between attackers and defenders in resource-constrained networks.
method: The authors develop a Game-Theory-Integrated Modified Multi-Wireless Sensor Epidemic Malware Propagation (GTI-mSEMP) framework and simulate three operational regimes: Balanced Matchup, Exploit Surge, and Hardened Defense.
result: Numerical simulations capture transient dynamics of susceptible and recovered node populations, showing how epidemic curves shift under different offensive/defensive efficiency advantages.
conclusion: The framework provides a rigorous foundation for evaluating dynamic malware propagation and predicting localized node population states in adversarial network environments.

title: Robust Harmful Features Under Jailbreak Attacks: Mechanistic Evidence From Attention Head Specialization In Large Language Models
authors: Yanchen Yin, Dongqi Han, Linghui Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Jailbreak attacks bypass LLM safety alignment, yet their mechanisms remain poorly understood. We provide evidence that attacks do not comprehensively eliminate safety features, but instead selectively suppress specific attention heads. We identify two functionally differentiated types: Adversarially Compromised Heads (ACHs) concentrated in early layers, which are suppressed under attacks, and Safety-Aligned Heads (SAHs) in mid-layers, which maintain robust activations even when attacks succeed. Ablation studies support the causal role of ACHs and the contribution of SAHs to robust activations: suppressing a small number of ACHs is sufficient to induce jailbreak-like behavior on normally refused inputs, while removing SAHs substantially weakens mid-layer safety activations. Token-level attribution further shows that ACH suppression is driven specifically by attack-template tokens, providing a mechanistic account of why attacks can bypass refusal decisions through ACH suppression while leaving internal safety signals sustained by SAHs -- a phenomenon we term Robust Harmful Features. To validate the practical significance of this robustness, we show that simply reading these persistent activations -- without any training -- yields competitive aggregate detection performance with strong adversarial robustness.
tldr: This paper studies jailbreak attacks on LLMs by analyzing attention head specialization, finding that attacks suppress specific heads while leaving robust safety features in mid-layers.
motivation: Understanding the mechanisms of jailbreak attacks is crucial for improving LLM safety alignment.
method: The authors identify two types of attention heads (ACHs and SAHs) through activation analysis and ablation studies, and use token-level attribution to explain attack suppression.
result: Suppressing a small number of ACHs induces jailbreak-like behavior, while SAHs maintain robust activations; reading these persistent activations yields competitive detection performance.
conclusion: Jailbreak attacks do not eliminate safety features but selectively suppress specific attention heads, revealing robust harmful features that can be leveraged for detection.

title: Buffered Control For Opacity In Timed Automata
authors: \'etienne Andr\'e, Sarah D\'epernet, Engel Lefaucheux
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Timed automata are an extension of finite automata that can measure and react to the passage of time, handling real-time constraints by using clocks. The timed opacity problem, where an attacker attempts to infer from observed actions and timestamps whether a secret location was visited, was shown undecidable for timed automata. Execution-time opacity is a decidable though limited setting in which the attacker attempts to detect whether the secret location was visited, by only relying on the run duration. Here, we significantly extend this setting, by allowing the attacker to observe all observable actions, in the right order though with only the integral parts of their timestamps, which we call buffered observations. We consider the controlled setting, in which we aim at dynamically defining a sequence of sets of enabled actions ensuring opacity with buffered observations. We first prove the inter-reducibility of full opacity (observations must not leak the visit of the secret location) and weak opacity (the attacker might prove that the location was not visited, but not that it was visited) in this new controlled setting. Then, we prove the undecidability of the problem of existence of a sequential control strategy ensuring opacity under buffered observations. Finally and most importantly, we prove that decidability is retrieved in two independent cases, with their tight theoretical complexities, with and without control. These two assumptions express realistic limitations of the controller. The first case is when the strategy of the controller changes at most an a priori fixed number of times per time unit, which is not a strong practical assumption. The second case is when all controllable actions are observable and distinguishable by an attacker.
tldr: This paper studies opacity in timed automata with buffered observations, proving undecidability and identifying decidable subcases.
motivation: Opacity is a security property ensuring that secret system states are not inferred by an attacker. The timed setting is challenging and previous work had limited attacker models.
method: The authors define a controlled timed automaton model with buffered observations (attacker sees actions and integer timestamps). They prove inter-reducibility of full and weak opacity, then show undecidability of control existence, and finally identify two decidable restrictions with tight complexity bounds.
result: The problem is undecidable in general, but becomes decidable under bounded-rate control strategies or when all controllable actions are observable and distinguishable.
conclusion: The work extends the theory of opacity in timed systems, providing fundamental limits and practical decidable cases for controller synthesis.

title: Non-Linear Strategic Classification Made Practical
authors: Jack Geary, Boyan Gao, Henry Gouk
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Algorithmic developments in Strategic Classification have been mostly limited to linear classifiers in settings where the best response has a closed-form solution or can be easily approximated. While some work has explored the role of non-linear classifiers in strategic settings, progress in this direction is impeded by the computational intractability of the strategic behaviour. Addressing this, we present a novel method for approximating the best response by exploiting Lagrangian duality. By reformulating the strategic response as a constrained optimisation problem, we can construct a Lagrangian that is amenable to first order optimisation methods. This approach reproduces closed-form strategic behaviour in linear settings and can be straight-forwardly applied to non-linear settings. We show how the Implicit Function Theorem can be used in conjunction with our proposed response formulation during classifier learning to compute the total gradient of the loss. This connects the classifier parameters directly to the consequent strategic behaviour, yielding a novel training algorithm that can exploit this relationship. Experimental evaluation shows that the resulting models achieve improved strategic accuracy on common machine learning datasets.
tldr: This paper proposes a method for approximating strategic best responses in non-linear classification using Lagrangian duality and implicit differentiation.
motivation: Strategic classification with non-linear classifiers is computationally intractable due to the difficulty of computing best responses.
method: The strategic response is reformulated as a constrained optimization problem, and a Lagrangian is constructed that can be solved with first-order methods. The Implicit Function Theorem is used to differentiate through the response during training.
result: The proposed method reproduces closed-form solutions in linear settings and extends to non-linear classifiers, achieving improved strategic accuracy on standard datasets.
conclusion: The approach makes non-linear strategic classification practical and effective.

title: Which Nash Equilibrium? Solver-Dependent Selection On Zero-Sum Nash Polytopes
authors: Luis Leal
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many two-player zero-sum games admit not a unique Nash equilibrium but a convex set of them: a polytope of profiles that all share the minimax value V* yet prescribe different behaviour. Standard solvers each converge to some equilibrium and are treated as interchangeable. We ask whether they instead select different members of the Nash set, systematically as a function of the algorithm rather than the seed. Using a tabular, exactly solvable testbed of six games with analytically known Nash sets -- including a two-dimensional Nash polytope and Kuhn poker -- we find that (i) selection is determined by the algorithm, not the seed, but families differ only on asymmetric Nash sets; (ii) regularized last-iterate methods (R-NaD, magnetic mirror descent) select the maximum-entropy member, the information projection of their uniform reference onto the Nash set -- exactly on the 2-D polytope and at 99.7% of maximum entropy in Kuhn -- while regret-averaging methods (CFR, CFR+, fictitious play) drift to a lower-entropy face; we confirm this on a randomized 180-game ensemble, where R-NaD attains the maximum-entropy member in 100% of converged games while CFR+ sits strictly below it in 94% (paired Wilcoxon p < 10^-27); (iii) the selected member has downstream consequences against sub-optimal opponents that scale with sequential/hidden-information structure but stay bounded -- in Kuhn the max-entropy member is a strictly better hedge, whereas on the matrix games the members differ without either dominating. We also report two negative results correcting common intuitions: removing CFR's positive-orthant (max(R,0)) projection does not eliminate boundary drift; and R-NaD's selection is anchor-following, not initialization-independent. We state the maximum-entropy / I-projection characterization as a strongly data-supported conjecture, checked throughout against analytic ground truth.
tldr: This paper studies algorithm-dependent selection of Nash equilibria in zero-sum games, focusing on solver behavior on Nash polytopes.
motivation: Standard solvers for zero-sum games are often treated as interchangeable, but they may converge to different Nash equilibria, which can have practical consequences.
method: The authors use tabular, exactly solvable testbeds including a 2D Nash polytope and Kuhn poker, comparing regularized last-iterate methods (R-NaD, magnetic mirror descent) with regret-averaging methods (CFR, CFR+, fictitious play).
result: Selection is algorithm-dependent; regularized methods select the maximum-entropy member, while regret-averaging methods drift to lower-entropy faces. The max-entropy member is a better hedge in sequential games.
conclusion: Algorithm choice systematically affects which Nash equilibrium is selected, with implications for downstream performance against sub-optimal opponents.

title: SidConArena: An Environment Evaluating Agents In Open-Ended,Positive-Sum Bargaining Game
authors: Yeqi Feng, Yuxin Chen, Tianxing He
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27397v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Evaluating LLM agents requires dynamic environments that go beyond static reasoning and zero-sum games. Real-world economic interaction is often open-ended and mixed-motive: agents must negotiate, create positive-sum surplus, compete for scarce assets, and plan under delayed returns. We introduce SidConArena, a new benchmark framework for evaluating LLM agents in open-ended, positive-sum bargaining. SidConArena formalizes a multi-player economy as a finite-horizon partially observable stochastic game with three coupled phases: natural-language negotiation with binding trades, deterministic converter-based production, and sealed-bid auctions for long-term assets. The framework combines structured observations, phase-aware agent dispatching, a neural-symbolic action interface, and asynchronous execution, enabling free-form interaction while preserving rule-grounded evaluation. Across homogeneous and heterogeneous tournaments, stronger frontier models achieve higher economic outcomes, yet agents still misvalue resources, bargain passively, and remain limited in long-horizon investment planning.
tldr: This paper introduces a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents in open-ended, positive-sum bargaining games, which is unrelated to quantum information theory.
motivation: The paper aims to create a dynamic environment for testing LLM agents in mixed-motive economic interactions, moving beyond static reasoning and zero-sum games.
method: SidConArena formalizes a multi-player economy as a finite-horizon partially observable stochastic game with negotiation, production, and auction phases, using a neural-symbolic action interface and asynchronous execution.
result: Stronger frontier models achieve higher economic outcomes, but agents still misvalue resources, bargain passively, and have limited long-horizon investment planning.
conclusion: The benchmark reveals limitations in current LLM agents for complex economic reasoning and planning.

title: Formal Grammars In Business Process Management: A Systematic Literature Review
authors: Milliam Maxime Zekeng Ndadji
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27399v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Business Process Management (BPM) is concerned with the systematic design, execution, monitoring, and improvement of business processes. Formal grammars have emerged as a particularly fruitful formalism for BPM, offering generative, declarative, and analytical capabilities that are uniquely well-suited to process-oriented concerns. This paper presents a systematic literature review of 34 primary studies at the intersection of formal grammars and BPM. We identify seven research streams: (i) process grammars for organizational process design; (ii) process modeling languages evaluated as grammars under the Bunge-Wand-Weber ontological framework; (iii) production-rule grammars for process structural specification and variant management; (iv) attribute grammars for the declarative specification and distributed execution of workflows; (v) graph grammars for the transformation, generation, and semantic analysis of process models; (vi) grammatical inference for process mining and discovery; and (vii) process algebras as grammar-like compositional frameworks for behavioral specification and verification. For each stream, we synthesize contributions, formalisms employed, and limitations. The review reveals that formal grammars have influenced BPM across every lifecycle phase (from organizational design to formal verification and data-driven discovery) yet the seven streams have developed largely in parallel, without cross-stream synthesis. We identify five corpus-grounded open challenges and argue that a deeper, unified exploitation of grammatical theory holds significant promise for advancing the state of the art in BPM.
tldr: A systematic literature review on the use of formal grammars in business process management.
motivation: To synthesize the fragmented research on formal grammars applied to BPM and identify open challenges.
method: Systematic literature review of 34 primary studies, categorizing them into seven research streams.
result: Identified seven research streams and five open challenges; found that streams have developed in parallel without cross-synthesis.
conclusion: A deeper, unified exploitation of grammatical theory could advance BPM, but current work is not directly relevant to quantum information theory or thermodynamics.

title: Productionized Fairness Measurement Under Privacy Constraints
authors: Osonde A. Osoba, Yuzi He, Saikrishna Badrinarayanan, Varun Mithal, Sakshi Jain, Natesh S. Pillai
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27558v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fairness measurements in the form of disaggregated evaluations often rely on demographic signals that are legally constrained or culturally sensitive. Race and ethnicity signals are among the more difficult signals to curate and use for this task. This paper presents Privacy-Preserving Probabilistic Race/Ethnicity Estimation (PPRE) as a method for enabling fairness measurements with respect to race/ethnicity for U.S.\ LinkedIn members in a privacy-preserving manner. PPRE applies privacy technologies (specifically: secure two-party computation, differential privacy, and additive homomorphic encryption) on top of two race/ethnicity demographic signal sources (the Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding estimator and a sparse golden survey set of self-reported demographics) to power a fairness measurement solution with respect to US-based race/ethnicity demographics. We detail its privacy guarantees and demonstrate its application on candidate- and viewer-side fairness measurements. We close with a transferable framework for institutions seeking to implement similar privacy-preserving measurement infrastructure.
tldr: This paper presents a privacy-preserving method for measuring fairness with respect to race/ethnicity on LinkedIn, using secure computation and differential privacy.
motivation: Fairness measurements often require sensitive demographic data, which is legally and culturally constrained. The authors aim to enable such measurements while protecting individual privacy.
method: They combine Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding with a sparse survey of self-reported demographics, and apply secure two-party computation, differential privacy, and additive homomorphic encryption to estimate race/ethnicity privately.
result: The method provides privacy guarantees and is demonstrated on candidate- and viewer-side fairness measurements for LinkedIn members.
conclusion: The paper offers a transferable framework for institutions to implement privacy-preserving fairness measurement infrastructure.

title: Halt Fast! Early Stopping For Certified Robustness
authors: Andrew C. Cullen, Paul Montague, Benjamin I. P. Rubinstein
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27694v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Randomized Smoothing (RS) provides rigorous robustness guarantees for neural networks without architectural constraints, yet its adoption is limited by extreme computational costs. Standard RS requires tens of thousands of model evaluations per input and forces practitioners to commit to fixed sample sizes a priori. In this work, we present a novel meta-learning framework for anytime-valid certified robustness that adaptively deploys computational resources. By using a lightweight meta-learner to predict image-specific priors for a sequential E-process, we achieve a 20-fold reduction in sample complexity compared to traditional methods while maintaining rigorous statistical guarantees. Beyond raw efficiency, we demonstrate how anytime-validity enables adaptively allocating compute based upon application-specific risk thresholds, a form of resource triage impossible under classic certification frameworks. That this is achievable while also providing similar certification performance demonstrates that our approach provides a pathway for real-time, safety-critical certification deployments.
tldr: This paper proposes a meta-learning framework for early stopping in randomized smoothing to achieve certified robustness with reduced sample complexity.
motivation: Standard randomized smoothing for certified robustness requires tens of thousands of model evaluations per input, making it computationally expensive and impractical for real-time applications.
method: A lightweight meta-learner predicts image-specific priors for a sequential E-process, enabling anytime-valid certification that adaptively allocates compute based on risk thresholds.
result: The approach achieves a 20-fold reduction in sample complexity while maintaining rigorous statistical guarantees and similar certification performance.
conclusion: The method provides a pathway for real-time, safety-critical certification deployments by enabling adaptive resource allocation.

title: Room For Error: Large-Scale Simulation Of Over-the-Air Acoustic Attacks
authors: Andrew C. Cullen, Neil Marchant, Jiani Xie, Paul Montague, Benjamin I. P. Rubinstein
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27701v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While voice control is rapidly becoming a ubiquitous vector of human-AI communication, the risks facing these systems remain poorly understood. This is, in part, a product of the difficulties in scaling strictly digital adversarial workflows to the physical world. These scale barriers have led the community to abstract away key acoustic factors relating to detectability and the influence of geometry on acoustics. These methodological and metrological shortcomings undermine our understanding of risk. We illuminate these issues through real-world testing, conceptual discussions, and a novel, high-throughput reality simulation framework. By testing over 8 million adversarial evaluations, we demonstrate that acoustic awareness yields relative Word Error Rate increases of up to 94.5\% under Whisper and wav2vec. We employ this framework to explore a formalize and operationalize a Dual-Form Signal to Noise Ratio to decouple source stealth from victim attack efficacy, resolving a crucial limitation in current works. This lays the groundwork for repeatable, verifiable research that embraces, rather than abstracts, the acoustic environment.
tldr: This paper studies acoustic adversarial attacks on voice control systems, focusing on simulation and detectability.
motivation: Voice control systems are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, but scaling digital attacks to the physical world is difficult and acoustic factors are often abstracted away.
method: The authors develop a high-throughput reality simulation framework and test over 8 million adversarial evaluations using Whisper and wav2vec models.
result: Acoustic awareness yields relative Word Error Rate increases of up to 94.5%, and a Dual-Form Signal to Noise Ratio is introduced to decouple source stealth from attack efficacy.
conclusion: The work lays groundwork for repeatable, verifiable research that embraces the acoustic environment in adversarial attacks.

title: Beating Trivial Time For Tricky Triangle Tasks
authors: Ryan Williams Neha Pant
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27727v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For several well-studied triangle detection problems in the literature, the trivial enumeration algorithms are known to be optimal (up to the exponent) assuming popular fine-grained conjectures. For example, All-Edges Sparse Triangle and Sparse Monochromatic Triangle where each node has degree [MATH] for some [MATH], and the Exact Triangle where edges have arbitrary weights, all have this property under the 3SUM Conjecture. However, as there are slightly nontrivial algorithms for 3SUM, it is natural to wonder if the trivial algorithm for these tricky triangle tasks might also be improved. Applying a variety of techniques from randomized algorithms, circuit complexity, and communication complexity, we present the first improvements over the trivial algorithms for each of these problems in the Word RAM model. Moreover, our algorithms can be implemented with only polysize [MATH] operations on words. Extending our techniques, we also show how to solve the notorious 4-cycle detection problem on [MATH]-node graphs in [MATH] time, in a Word-RAM model with word size [MATH]. Along the way, we show how to sort [MATH] items over a universe of size [MATH] using only [MATH] word operations in [MATH] time.
tldr: This paper presents improved algorithms for triangle detection problems and 4-cycle detection in the Word RAM model, using techniques from randomized algorithms, circuit complexity, and communication complexity.
motivation: The trivial enumeration algorithms for several triangle detection problems are believed to be optimal under fine-grained conjectures, but the authors aim to find non-trivial improvements.
method: The authors apply a variety of techniques including randomized algorithms, circuit complexity, and communication complexity to design new algorithms for All-Edges Sparse Triangle, Sparse Monochromatic Triangle, Exact Triangle, and 4-cycle detection.
result: They present the first improvements over trivial algorithms for these problems in the Word RAM model, with algorithms implementable using only polysize word operations.
conclusion: The results show that non-trivial improvements are possible for these problems, challenging the optimality of trivial algorithms.

title: Triadic Werewolf: A Jester Role For Multi-Hop Theory Of Mind In LLMs
authors: Avni Mittal
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27909v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Theory-of-mind evaluations of large language models typically use dyadic social-deduction games, where every observable cue points to a single hidden side, so a model with strong language priors can score well without ever simulating opponents' incentives. We extend the Werewolf game with a Jester, a third faction whose utility on peer suspicion is inverted because it wins by being voted out, so optimal play requires reasoning across three opposing utility functions. Across 60 games on GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3.1, and Llama-3.3-70B with Jester self-learning on and off, the Jester wins 60-70% of games while Werewolves never exceed 20%, and GPT-4.1 wolves vote the Jester out on day 1 in 60-70% of games, a strictly self-defeating action. Self-learning helps DeepSeek and Llama but hurts GPT-4.1, with the cost landing on Villagers rather than Werewolves. Only DeepSeek learns the subtle strategy of looking suspicious without looking intentionally suspicious, and it gains the most from the loop. Triadic incentive structure exposes a layer of multi-agent reasoning that dyadic deduction games leave invisible.
tldr: This paper extends the Werewolf social-deduction game with a Jester role to evaluate theory of mind in LLMs, finding that triadic incentive structures reveal reasoning failures not visible in dyadic games.
motivation: Standard theory-of-mind evaluations using dyadic games may be gamed by language priors; a third faction with inverted utility exposes deeper multi-agent reasoning.
method: The authors implement a triadic Werewolf variant with a Jester role, run 60 games on GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3.1, and Llama-3.3-70B with and without self-learning, and analyze win rates and voting patterns.
result: The Jester wins 60-70% of games; Werewolves never exceed 20%; GPT-4.1 wolves self-defeatingly vote out the Jester on day 1 in 60-70% of games; self-learning helps DeepSeek and Llama but hurts GPT-4.1.
conclusion: Triadic incentive structures expose a layer of multi-agent reasoning that dyadic games miss, and current LLMs struggle with optimal play under conflicting utilities.

title: How Humans, Bots, And Agents Communicate About Vulnerabilities In Pull Requests
authors: Pien Rooijendijk, Christoph Treude, Mairieli Wessel
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28125v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Developers may reference vulnerabilities in pull request discussions through both explicit identifiers, such as CVEs or GHSAs, and implicit security-related language (e.g., "unauthorized access" or "SQL injection"). Prior work has primarily focused on explicit identifiers, potentially overlooking vulnerability discussions that lack formal references. Bots and coding agents are becoming more common in pull requests, raising new questions about how different accounts communicate about vulnerabilities. In this registered report, we describe our planned study of vulnerability communication in pull requests by humans, bots, and coding agents. Building on the AIDev-pop dataset, we analyze explicit vulnerability references and implicit security-related signals across pull request titles, descriptions, review comments, commit messages, and timeline discussions. We further investigate whether these references are associated with vulnerabilities introduced or fixed in the modified code and how they relate to pull request review activity and outcomes. This study contributes a large-scale empirical investigation of vulnerability communication practices in modern software development.
tldr: This paper studies how humans, bots, and coding agents communicate about vulnerabilities in pull request discussions, focusing on explicit and implicit security references.
motivation: Prior work has overlooked implicit vulnerability references and the role of automated agents in pull request discussions.
method: The authors plan to analyze the AIDev-pop dataset, examining explicit vulnerability identifiers and implicit security-related language across various pull request components.
result: The study is a registered report; results are not yet available.
conclusion: The research aims to provide a large-scale empirical investigation of vulnerability communication practices in modern software development.

title: AI-Driven Synthesis For High-Tech System Design: Automating Innovation
authors: Luuk Oerlemans, Steven Westerhof, Theo Hofman
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28126v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This article addresses the combinatorial complexity inherent in modern high-tech system design by presenting automation-in-design (AiD) as a transformative paradigm. We propose computational design synthesis (CDS), a framework utilising deep learning and generative AI to automate the creation of novel systems. Two case studies (e-drive system design and spatial dimensioning problem) serve as proof-points for this approach. The AI-driven methods used in the case studies represent a fundamental shift in engineering, advancing from simulation-based optimisation towards autonomous design with minimal human supervision.
tldr: This paper presents an AI-driven framework for automating high-tech system design, focusing on engineering optimization rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The combinatorial complexity of modern high-tech system design requires new automation paradigms to reduce human supervision and accelerate innovation.
method: The authors propose computational design synthesis (CDS) using deep learning and generative AI, demonstrated through two case studies: e-drive system design and spatial dimensioning.
result: The AI-driven methods enable autonomous design with minimal human intervention, showing a fundamental shift from simulation-based optimization.
conclusion: Automation-in-design (AiD) can transform engineering by leveraging AI to handle complex design spaces, but the work is unrelated to quantum information theory or thermodynamics.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures

abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.

motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-power devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of breakdown initiation.
result: They identify that tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact to trigger breakdowns.
conclusion: These insights can help improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.

Hadron spectroscopy is a frontier of particle physics; searching for new hadrons is crucial for validating the theory of strong interaction (QCD). Investigating how charmonium, a bound state of charm and anticharm quarks, decays and searching for new charmoniumlike states yield valuable insights into strong interaction mechanisms, including quark confinement and gluon binding. Hadrons produced at e− collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs are a primary source of experimental information for these investigations. This Colloquium reviews current progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments. As BESIII accumulates high-precision data, it has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems, and recent advances are highlighted.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021001] Published Fri Apr 03, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews hadron production in open-charm meson pairs at e+e- colliders, focusing on charmonium spectroscopy and strong interaction mechanisms.
motivation: Searching for new hadrons and understanding charmonium decays provides insights into QCD, quark confinement, and gluon binding.
method: The paper reviews experimental progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments, highlighting recent advances from BESIII.
result: BESIII has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems with high-precision data.
conclusion: The review summarizes current knowledge and recent advances in hadron production from open-charm meson pairs, contributing to hadron spectroscopy.
